docs.title: Gesso
docs.text:
Gesso — the primer layer a painter applies before the artwork.

Gesso is an SDK for building Qt (PySide6) desktop applications on Linux. It provides the parts every application needs and nobody wants to write twice, so you can spend your time on the part that is actually yours.

Muralis — a wallpaper manager — is the first application built on it. Gesso is the primer; Muralis is the mural.

docs.text:
Gesso is layered by dependency weight. A command-line tool can use the core and pay for nothing else; a full desktop application opts into Qt explicitly.

        A[ui.app<br/><small>bootstrap & shell</small>]

Dependencies only ever point downward, and the application sits on top. Gesso never imports your application.

docs.title: The one rule
docs.text:
An application depends on Gesso. Gesso never depends on the application.

Everything in Gesso is parameterised by an :class:~gesso.core.AppSpec that you supply — its name, its id, its version. That is what lets the same code serve Muralis, your next application, and a test suite, without any of them reaching for ~/.config/<something> that only one of them should own.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/QHaidry/gesso.git
cd gesso
python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
pytest                       # everything
pytest tests/test_store.py   # one file
pytest -k convert            # by name

The suite should be green before you push. Two tests skip when tomli-w is absent; installing the dev extra gives you full coverage, including the TOML write path and the TOML-only branches of discovery.

docs.title: Building the docs
docs.text:
mkdocs serve    # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict

--strict is the real check: it turns warnings into failures, so a broken internal link or a missing snippet file will stop the build. Run it before pushing.

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
The rule in Architecture is not a guideline:

An application depends on Gesso. Gesso never depends on the application.

Concretely: no module in gesso may import from an application, and gesso.core and gesso.config must not import Qt. If you find yourself needing an application's name, take an AppSpec instead.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Keep the core dependency-free. A new third-party import belongs behind an optional extra, and its codec or feature must degrade with an actionable unavailable_reason() rather than an ImportError at an unrelated place.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Type hints on public functions.
  • 100-column lines, black formatting.
  • Docstrings explain why, not what — the code already says what.
  • Comments are for the non-obvious: a specification quirk, a workaround, a deliberate refusal.

docs.title: Documentation is part of the contract
docs.text:
An SDK is its documentation. Two rules keep the two from drifting apart:

  1. Examples are executed. examples/hello.py is driven by tests/test_example.py, and the guide embeds the real file via pymdownx.snippets. If the example breaks, the docs are wrong and the suite says so.
  2. mkdocs build --strict must pass. Snippets use check_paths, so a typo in an embedded path fails the build rather than silently rendering nothing.

If you change a public API, update the matching page under docs/reference/.

docs.title: Adding a codec
docs.text:
1. Subclass Codec in gesso/config/codecs.py, defining name, extensions, loads and dumps.
  2. Gate it with available() / unavailable_reason(), naming the package to install.
  3. Add it to the _CODECS tuple and, if it should win ties, to DISCOVERY_PRECEDENCE.
  4. Add the dependency as an optional extra in pyproject.toml, and to dev so the tests always run it.
  5. Extend tests/test_codecs.py.

Because the schema is codec-independent, nothing else needs to change — that is the point of the split.

docs.title: The guide
docs.text:
Gesso has a lot of pages. This one tells you which to read, and in what order, for whatever you are actually trying to do.

Everything here is a signpost. If you already know what you want, the sidebar and the reference are faster.

docs.title: If you have five minutes
docs.text:
$ pip install -e .
$ gesso new myapp
$ cd myapp && python -m myapp

A window, wired up. Quickstart is the same thing with the parts explained.

I am starting a projectI want to understand the designI want to do one specific thingI am learning by reading code

  2. Quickstart — gesso new, and what it generates.
  3. Application identity — the AppSpec, and why every path comes from it.
  4. Then Tracker, which is what a filled-in project looks like.

You do not need to read the concepts first. The generated project is small, and reading it is faster than reading about it.

Read Architecture first — the tier rule ("an application depends on Gesso; Gesso never depends on the application") and the Qt-free/optional-dependency boundaries explain almost every other decision in the SDK.

Read the four examples in order. Each rung adds a tier and keeps the one below it, so reading them adds up to reading Gesso's feature set:

docs.title: Two things to know before you write anything
docs.text:
The tier rule. An application depends on Gesso. Gesso never depends on the application. That is why there is no global singleton, why AppContext is something you construct and pass, and why nothing under gesso.core or gesso.config imports Qt.

Nothing says "application". There is no Application base class to inherit, no plugin registry, and no framework lifecycle. Gesso supplies identity, settings, translations, a design system and a window; your code is everything else, and it stays ordinary Python. See Architecture.

docs.title: If something is missing
docs.text: The roadmap says what is planned and, more usefully, what is deliberately not. Reach for the contributing guide if you think something belongs here — the bar is usually "does a second application need it?".

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The order is deliberate: each tier is proven by an application before the next one is designed.

docs.title: 1. Larger widget composites — gesso.ui.widgets
docs.text:
The primitives are in. What is deliberately not here:

  • Composites — NavSidebar, SettingsExplorer, ThumbnailGrid, SearchField, Callout
  • Dialogs — info, warning, critical, confirm, FormDialog
  • SettingsPage — driven by a schema, so declaring your options gives you a complete settings UI

These wait for a second application to need the same shape. The primitives were safe to build because the base stylesheet already named them; composites would mean designing an API for a shape nobody has built yet.

docs.title: 2. Migrations
docs.text: A declarative schema-version mechanism, replacing the explicit manual migrations used today.

docs.title: 3. An optional internationalisation backend
docs.text:
Two things gesso.i18n deliberately does not do, because doing them properly needs real CLDR data and guessing is worse than waiting:

  • Plural rules. English's one/other split is not how Polish, Arabic or Russian work.
  • Locale-aware number and date formatting. 1234567.89 is written differently in Germany, India and the United States.

These ship as an optional extra, so the dependency-free core stays dependency-free. The catalog contract is already narrow — catalog(language) -> dict — so a gettext or Qt .qm backend can be added without changing the public API.

docs.title: Adjacent, not yet scheduled
docs.text:
Broadly useful, but outside the original five features. Candidates for an optional gesso.extras layer:

  • Systemd user timers / cron scheduling
  • Storage retention and cleanup
  • Downloads with proxies and retries
  • Desktop notifications

docs.title: What Gesso will not do
docs.text:
Stating this keeps the SDK from bloating:

  • No plugin framework. Extension is constructor arguments and subclassing.
  • No global application singleton. AppContext is something you construct, including in tests — and there is no process-wide Translator either.
  • No domain code. If it is specific to your product, it belongs to your product.
  • No framework lock-in. Gesso is a library you call; it does not run your application for you.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text:
Most small applications hard-code where their files live:

CONFIG_PATH = Path.home() / ".config" / "myapp" / "config.json"
WALLPAPER_DIR = Path.home() / "Pictures" / "MyApp"

It works right up until it doesn't. The application cannot be tested without touching the developer's real home directory. It cannot be run with a throwaway profile. A second application cannot reuse a line of it. And the day the name changes, the paths are wrong in a dozen files.

Gesso replaces all of that with one declaration.

docs.title: AppSpec — who the application is
docs.text:
APP = AppSpec(
    name="Gesso Hello",
    app_id="gesso-hello",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="A tiny example application built on Gesso.",
    default_config_format="json",
)
Field Type Default Meaning name str required Human-readable name, e.g. "Gesso Hello" app_id str slug of name Directory name, window class, systemd unit org str "" Organisation, for desktop integration version str "0.0.0" Application version display_name str name Name shown in the UI description str "" One-line description default_config_format str "json" Format used when creating a config config_stem str "config" Filename stem, before the extension

AppSpec is a frozen dataclass: once built it cannot be mutated, so nothing can quietly rewrite your application's identity halfway through a run.

app_id is derived from name when you do not supply it:

>>> from gesso.core import AppSpec, slugify
>>> AppSpec("My Fancy App").app_id
'my-fancy-app'
>>> slugify("Muralis")
'muralis'

Use an explicit app_id

Slugifying is a convenience for examples and tests. A real application should state its id, because changing it later moves the user's files:

AppSpec(name="Muralis", app_id="muralis", org="Acme", version="0.4.0")

docs.title: AppPaths — where the files go
docs.text:
Gesso follows the XDG Base Directory specification.

Property Base Default Holds config_dir $XDG_CONFIG_HOME ~/.config Settings, themes, locale overrides data_dir $XDG_DATA_HOME ~/.local/share Durable application data cache_dir $XDG_CACHE_HOME ~/.cache Regenerable caches state_dir $XDG_STATE_HOME ~/.local/state Logs, session state

Each is the base joined with app_id:

flowchart LR
    H["$XDG_CONFIG_HOME<br/><small>~/.config</small>"]
    A["app_id<br/><small>myapp</small>"]
    R["~/.config/myapp"]
    H --> A --> R
$ tree --dirsfirst ~/.config/myapp ~/.cache/myapp
~/.config/myapp
├── config.json
└── themes/
~/.cache/myapp
└── thumbnails/

Three specification details Gesso gets right, because they are easy to get wrong:

  • An unset variable falls back to the default.
  • An empty variable falls back to the default (not to "").
  • A relative path is ignored, because the specification requires an absolute one. Gesso will not silently resolve config against your current working directory.

docs.title: AppContext — the two, bound together
docs.text:
AppContext pairs an AppSpec with its resolved AppPaths. This is the object the rest of Gesso accepts, so no other module ever has to know how to find your files.

from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec

context = AppContext(AppSpec("My App", app_id="myapp"))

context.app_id      # 'myapp'
context.config_dir  # PosixPath('/home/you/.config/myapp')
context.config_file()          # .../config.json   (uses default_config_format)
context.config_file("toml")    # .../config.toml

docs.title: Isolated profiles
docs.text:
Because the base directories are stored on AppPaths rather than read from the environment on every access, you can point an application at a throwaway tree without mutating os.environ — which is what makes Gesso testable:

from pathlib import Path

from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec
from gesso.core.paths import AppPaths

spec = AppSpec("My App", app_id="myapp")
paths = AppPaths.resolve(spec.app_id, config_home=Path("/tmp/profile-a"))
context = AppContext(spec, paths)

assert context.config_dir == Path("/tmp/profile-a/myapp")

Two contexts built this way never collide, so tests can run in parallel and without cleaning up after themselves.

docs.title: The application shell
docs.text:
Almost every desktop application is the same window: a list of destinations down one side, a page for each, and a strip of live information along the bottom. Almost every application implements it slightly differently, and gets the collapsible-sidebar details slightly wrong.

Gesso ships that window, and the few lines of start-up that go around it.

docs.title: Starting up
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.app import run_app


def build(shell):
    shell.add_page("home", "Home", HomePage(), icon="folder")
    shell.set_brand("My App", "does one thing well")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(run_app(APP, build))

run_app does five things, each of which every Qt application does slightly differently:

Step Why it is not trivial Build the QApplication The name and organisation are what Qt uses to locate settings, and what the window manager shows in the task switcher Set the layout direction An RTL language mirrors the entire interface, and Qt does it without a single widget knowing Apply the theme Stylesheet and palette — see the design system Build the window build populates the shell, or returns a window of its own Install an exception hook This is the one everybody forgets

The forgotten step

A Qt application whose slot raises prints a traceback to stderr and carries on. When the application was launched from a menu, that stderr goes nowhere — the user sees a button that did nothing, and there is no record of why.

run_app installs a hook that logs the traceback and hands it to your on_error so you can show it. KeyboardInterrupt is left to Python, which is what Ctrl-C in a terminal expects.

No high-DPI setup, deliberately

Qt 6 scales high-DPI displays by default. The Qt 5 attributes that used to enable it are deprecated no-ops that only produce warnings, so Gesso does not set them.

docs.title: The shell
docs.text:
shell.add_page("settings", tr("Settings"), SettingsPage(), icon="settings",
               comment=tr("Providers and storage."), actions=(apply_button,))

add_page creates both the navigation entry and the page body, so the two cannot drift apart. It returns the Page, and shell.header(key) gives you the header row afterwards if a title or an action needs to change later.

Pages are addressed by a stable key, so a translated title never becomes an identifier.

docs.title: Collapsing
docs.text: Collapsing the sidebar narrows it to icons. It also keeps every label as a tooltip — icon-only navigation with no labels and no tooltips is a memory test, not an interface. The collapsed layout is keyed off a collapsed property on the button, so the button is repolished when it changes; without that the stylesheet never notices.

docs.title: The payoff from the theme tier
docs.text:
themes.apply("light")   # navigation icons re-tint themselves

The shell connects to ThemeManager.themeChanged and repaints its navigation icons, giving the checked entry the accent. That is the whole reason the signal exists: without it, every application has to remember to refresh its icons at every call site, and the failure mode — an icon left at the old colour until something else happens to redraw it — is subtle enough to ship.

docs.title: What the shell deliberately is not
docs.text:
• Not a framework you subclass into. It is a window you populate. If you need a different window, return one from build and the shell goes unused.
  • Not a settings UI. SettingsExplorer and a schema-driven SettingsPage are on the roadmap, waiting for a second application to need the same shape.
  • Not Qt's translation system. Gesso's i18n reads JSON catalogs directly, so there is nothing to install into Qt; QTranslator and .qm files are a different mechanism and would arrive as an optional backend.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Gesso is organised in tiers, layered by dependency weight. The goal is simple: a command-line tool should pay nothing for a graphical toolkit it will never open.

docs.title: The dependency rule
docs.text:
An application depends on Gesso. Gesso never depends on the application.

Everything Gesso needs to know about your application arrives as an :class:~gesso.core.AppSpec. Gesso never imports your code, never reads a hard-coded path for you, and never assumes there is only one application in the world. Break this rule and the SDK stops being reusable; it becomes a framework you are trapped inside.

docs.title: What Gesso deliberately does not do
docs.text:
An SDK earns its keep by what it refuses to include. Gesso has no opinion about:

  • Your domain. No wallpapers, no documents, no editor buffers. Those belong to the application.
  • Your dependency injection. Gesso takes plain constructor arguments; it does not require a container or a plugin registry.
  • Your framework. AppContext is an ordinary object you can construct in a test, not a global you have to mock.

docs.title: How an application plugs in
docs.text:
Every tier takes the same small handle — an AppContext — so wiring an application is a two-step affair:

from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec

spec = AppSpec("My App", app_id="myapp", version="1.0.0")  # who
context = AppContext(spec)                                 # who + where

Pass context to whatever you need, and construct it with an injected AppPaths when you want an isolated profile (tests, portable installs):

from gesso.core.paths import AppPaths

sandboxed = AppContext(spec, AppPaths.resolve(spec.app_id, config_home=tmp_path))

That is the whole extension mechanism. There is no plugin API to learn because there is no framework to fight.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Gesso's configuration layer does one unusual thing: it types your values. Everything else follows from that.

docs.title: Why typing is not a detail
docs.text:
Most small applications store settings as strings, because the file format they grew up with (configparser) only has strings:

[general]
auto_update = true     ; the string "true"
interval = 86400       ; the string "86400"

Then every read site has to remember to convert, and one of them eventually forgets. Worse, the moment you offer a modern format the bug becomes visible and embarrassing — because in TOML this is a real boolean and this is a string:

auto_update = true      # bool
auto_update = "true"    # str — and it is truthy either way, until it isn't

Gesso makes the type part of the declaration, and coerces at the boundary.

docs.title: The three objects
docs.text:
SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "greeting",
            title="Greeting",
            description="How the application greets you.",
            options=(
                Option("name", str, "World", "Who to greet."),
                Option("punctuation", str, "!", "Appended to the greeting."),
                Option("shout", bool, False, "Print the greeting in UPPERCASE."),
                Option("repeat", int, 1, "How many times to print the greeting."),
            ),
        )
    ]
)
Object Role Option One setting: key, type, default, description Section A named group of options — one table in the file Schema The ordered collection of sections: your whole contract

docs.title: Types you can declare
docs.text:
type Accepts Rejects bool True, 1, "true", "yes", "on", "enabled" (and falsey equivalents) "maybe" int 42, "42", 3.0 "abc", True float 1.5, 2, "1.5" "abc", True str anything scalar (True → "true", 7 → "7") containers list list, tuple "a,b" dict dict anything else 
>>> from gesso.config import Option
>>> Option("auto_update", bool, True).coerce("false")
False
>>> Option("interval", int, 86400).coerce("3600")
3600

bool is checked before int

In Python bool is a subclass of int, so True would happily be read as the integer 1. Gesso refuses that conversion on purpose — a boolean is not an integer, and silently accepting one is how "1" ends up in a "number" field.

docs.title: The lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant App
    participant Store as ConfigStore
    participant Codec
    participant Disk

    App->>Store: discover(schema, config_dir)
    Store->>Disk: look for config.{json,toml,yaml}
    Disk-->>Store: found, or nothing
    App->>Store: load()
    Store->>Disk: read text
    Store->>Codec: loads(text)
    Codec-->>Store: plain dict
    Store->>Store: overlay on schema defaults, coerce each value
    Note over Store: unknown keys are kept, not dropped
    App->>Store: get("editor.font_size")
    App->>Store: set("editor.font_size", "15")
    Store->>Store: coerce to int
    App->>Store: save()
    Store->>Codec: dumps(data)
    Store->>Disk: temp file + atomic rename

docs.title: Two guarantees worth stating plainly
docs.text:
Loading never destroys data. A key the schema has never heard of, or a value that will not coerce, is preserved rather than dropped. Problems are reported by validate(); they are not silenced by deleting the evidence. A configuration file is the user's, and a loader that prunes it is a loader that loses data.

Saving is atomic. Writes go to a temporary file in the same directory and are then os.replaced over the target. A crash, a full disk, or a SIGKILL mid-write leaves the old configuration intact rather than a half-written one.

>>> store.load()
>>> store.get("editor.font_size")
13
>>> store.set("editor.font_size", "huge")
ConfigError: editor.font_size: cannot read 'huge' as an integer

set raises immediately rather than storing junk, so the failure surfaces at the call site instead of on the next launch.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
validate() returns a list of human-readable problems — empty means valid.

>>> store.validate()
[]
>>> for problem in store.validate():
...     print("warning:", problem)
warning: unknown option editor.mystery
warning: editor.font_size: cannot read 'huge' as an integer

Missing keys are not problems: they are filled from the schema defaults, so a partial — or even empty — file is perfectly legal and always upgradeable.

docs.title: Where the file is, and in what format
docs.text:
Format is a property of the file, resolved once when the store is built. See Choosing a config format for the full resolution order and the reasoning behind it.

Constructor Use when ConfigStore.for_app(schema, context) Normal use — discover within the app's config directory ConfigStore.discover(schema, directory, ...) You have a directory but no AppContext ConfigStore.for_format(schema, directory, fmt) The user explicitly chose a format ConfigStore.for_path(schema, path) You have an exact file in mind

docs.title: Design system and theming
docs.text:
A design system is a contract, not a stylesheet. The contract says which names exist, what each means, and what happens when one is missing. A stylesheet is merely one consumer of it.

Getting that order right is the difference between a theme that reports a problem and a theme that silently loses a rule — and an interface that mysteriously collapses to the platform default.

docs.title: The token contract
docs.text:
A token is a named design decision. Gesso ships one contract covering the 30 tokens an interface needs, grouped for documentation and for a settings UI:

Group Tokens surfaces window, panel, card, card_hover, preview_bg, menu_bg, nav_active_bg, tooltip_bg text text_strong, text, text_muted, text_disabled, tooltip_text accent accent, accent_hover, accent_text, selection buttons btn_bg, btn_hover, btn_active borders border, border_strong inputs input_bg, input_border, focus_border scroll scroll_handle, scroll_handle_hover menu menu_hover status status_bg, status_text

Every token carries a last-resort default, so a theme that sets nothing at all still renders a coherent interface:

from gesso.ui.theme import BASE_CONTRACT, render

sheet = render(BASE_CONTRACT.defaults(), {"icon_dir": "/path/to/icons"})

That is why a partial theme is a legitimate theme rather than an error. Set the three tokens you care about and inherit the rest:

{ "colors": { "accent": "#e8590c", "accent_hover": "#d9480f" } }

docs.title: The two failure modes
docs.text: Both are silent without help, and both are reported here.

docs.title: A misspelt token
docs.text:
{ "colors": { "acccent": "#e8590c" } }

Nothing in Qt complains: the stylesheet substitutes accent from the default, and the accent quietly stays violet with no explanation. Gesso reports it:

>>> manager.problems("oops")
["unknown token 'acccent'"]

docs.title: A missing token
docs.text:
The stylesheet's required tokens are derived from the stylesheet itself, so the list cannot drift from the contract:

>>> from gesso.ui.theme import placeholders
>>> placeholders()[:3]
('accent', 'accent_hover', 'accent_text')

Every missing token, not just the first

Qt's own string.Template.substitute raises on the first token it cannot find, which turns one broken palette into a sequence of one-at-a-time discoveries. Gesso names them all at once:

QssError: the stylesheet needs tokens that were not provided:
accent, accent_text, window

docs.title: The stylesheet
docs.text:
base.qss is shipped with the package and is entirely token-driven — nothing in it hard-codes a colour, so a theme is a data change rather than a fork of the file.

It also defines the object-name contract: widgets set an object name, and the stylesheet styles it. #pageHeader, #navButton, #primaryButton, #toggleButton, #iconButton, #card, #thumbFrame, #emptyState and the rest are public names the widget library will rely on. Styling a standard widget never means writing more stylesheet.

string.Template has no escaping

A placeholder written inside a CSS comment is still substituted, and will demand a token that does not exist. This is not hypothetical — it is how the base stylesheet first broke, and a test now asserts that every placeholder in it is a real token.

docs.title: Theming
docs.text:
A theme is a JSON palette. Palettes are loaded in layers, lowest priority first, so an application can build on Gesso's and a user can override both:

flowchart LR
    C["Contract defaults"]
    B["Built-in palettes<br/><small>gesso shipped, then the app's</small>"]
    U["User overrides<br/><small>~/.config/<app>/themes</small>"]
    R["Resolved theme"]
    C --> B --> U --> R
from pathlib import Path

from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager

manager = ThemeManager(
    app,
    builtin_dirs=[Path("myapp/themes")],           # layered over Gesso's
    user_dir=context.paths.subdir("config", "themes"),
)
manager.apply("dark")

Because each layer only overrides what it sets, a stale user theme missing a newly added token still renders: the missing key falls through to the built-in value.

docs.title: Reacting to a theme change
docs.text:
manager.themeChanged.connect(self._retint_icons)

Widgets re-tint on a change, so applying the same theme twice does not emit. That signal is why themed icons no longer have to be refreshed by hand at every call site — the failure mode being an icon that stays the old colour until something else happens to redraw it.

docs.title: Stylesheet and palette
docs.text: apply() sets both. Qt draws tooltips, menu frames and other native furniture from the QPalette, not from the stylesheet, so setting only the stylesheet leaves those pieces at the platform default — which is how a carefully themed application ends up with a yellow tooltip.

docs.title: A note on discoverability and deleted themes
docs.text:
Two details that only show up once a real application uses this.

Seeding. A user cannot edit a theme they cannot see, so seed_user_dir() copies the built-in palettes into the user's directory. Copies are only written where nothing exists, so an edit is never clobbered — and a later release of an application cannot silently undo a customisation. It is opt-in (seed=True), because an application that wants its palettes to stay read-only should say so.

Falling back. apply() falls back to the default theme when the requested name has no palette installed. Without it, deleting your theme file would leave the application wearing a neutral palette nobody chose — the tokens all resolve, so nothing looks broken, it just looks like a different application.

docs.title: The tier boundary
docs.text:
The token contract and the renderer are Qt-free. Substituting tokens into text needs no toolkit, so a palette can be checked without opening a window or installing PySide6. The manager, which touches QApplication and QPalette, is imported lazily on first use:

from gesso.ui.theme import BASE_CONTRACT, render   # no Qt
from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager            # needs Qt

import gesso must never pull in a toolkit, and a test runs a subprocess to prove it — within a test process Qt is already loaded, so a subprocess is the only honest check.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text: Icons follow the same rule as the rest of the design system: one asset, every theme. An SVG is rendered into a pixmap and tinted at request time, so adding a theme never means adding a second copy of the artwork — which is exactly what a set of fixed-colour icons forces you to do.

docs.title: Tinting
docs.text:
Tinting is a composition, not an edit to the SVG source. The artwork is drawn, then CompositionMode_SourceIn replaces its colour while preserving its alpha:

registry = IconRegistry()
pixmap = registry.render_pixmap("check", size=24, tint="#ff0000")

That is why the stroke colour inside the shipped SVGs does not matter, and why one file renders correctly at every size.

Pass tint=None to keep the artwork's own colours — the right choice for a multi-colour logo, where flattening to one colour would lose the design.

docs.title: Roles, not colours
docs.text:
An icon is requested by role, and the role decides which token it draws its colour from:

Role Token For idle text_muted A resting toolbar or navigation icon strong text Emphasised icon active accent The selected or primary action disabled text_disabled An unavailable action on-accent accent_text An icon sitting on an accent fill

Naming roles by purpose rather than by colour is what lets a theme decide what "active" looks like without anything else changing.

docs.title: Icons that follow the theme
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.icons import ThemedIcons
from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager

themes = ThemeManager(app)
icons = ThemedIcons(theme_manager=themes)

button.setIcon(icons.make_icon("refresh", role="active"))

ThemedIcons connects to the manager's themeChanged signal and re-emits iconsChanged, so a widget holding an icon can rebuild it without knowing why.

Why this signal matters

When tinting is done by hand at each call site, switching theme leaves every icon at its old colour until something else happens to redraw it — an interface that is subtly wrong, and hard to attribute to anything. The signal removes the class of bug rather than the instance.

Before any theme has been applied, a role still resolves — to the token contract's default, which is the same value the stylesheet will use. An icon built during start-up, before the first apply(), is therefore not visibly different from one built after it.

docs.title: Adding your own icons
docs.text:
IconRegistry searches directories in order, later ones winning, so an application layers its own icons over Gesso's without forking the set:

registry = IconRegistry()
registry.add_directory(Path("myapp/icons"))

A missing icon names the alternatives rather than rendering nothing:

IconError: no icon named 'refrsh'; available icons: check, chevron-down, ...

That message is the point. A reference to an icon that is not shipped renders as nothing at all — no error, no placeholder, just a control that is quietly missing its picture.

docs.title: The shipped set
docs.text:
Gesso ships a deliberately small starter set: chevrons in four directions, check, close, plus, minus, refresh, search, warning and info. The machinery is the deliverable; adding an SVG to the directory is the whole of "adding an icon".

The base stylesheet already references chevron-up and chevron-down for the spin-box arrows, and a test asserts that every icon the stylesheet references exists — the same drift check the token contract gets.

docs.title: Internationalisation
docs.text: Translation catalogs are JSON, looked up by dotted key, and merged from three layers so that neither the framework nor the application can accidentally trample the other — or the user.

docs.title: Three layers, in priority order
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["1 · Framework<br/><small>gesso.* keys</small>"]
    A["2 · Application<br/><small>your locales/</small>"]
    U["3 · User<br/><small>~/.config/<app>/i18n/</small>"]
    R["Resolved catalog"]
    U --> A --> F --> R
    classDef layer fill:#eceff1,stroke:#607d8b,color:#263238
    class F,A,U layer
Layer Where it lives Who owns it Framework gesso/i18n/locales/<lang>.json, shipped in the package Gesso Application your own locales/ directory You User $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/<app_id>/i18n/<lang>.json The user, at runtime

Later layers win. That is the whole override mechanism — no special cases, and no way for the user's file to lose to a newer release of your application's built-in strings.

docs.title: The reserved gesso.* domain
docs.text:
Gesso's own strings live under a gesso. prefix. Yours live under anything else. Because the prefix namespaces are disjoint, a merge can never collide:

{ "gesso": { "button": { "cancel": "Cancel" } } }

{ "myapp": { "menu": { "file": "File" } } }

translator.t("gesso.button.cancel")   # 'Cancel'  — the framework's
translator.t("myapp.menu.file")       # 'File'    — yours

Without this, every application would inherit the framework's key names and eventually collide with them.

docs.title: Language detection
docs.text:
The active language is read from the environment, in this order:

# Source Notes 1 LANGUAGE The only variable defined as a colon-separated priority list; the first entry wins 2 LC_ALL Overrides everything below it by definition 3 LC_MESSAGES 4 LANG 5 the C library locale What every other application on the system is using 6 "en" The fallback

A locale string is reduced to a two-letter code, so en_US.UTF-8, en-US and en are all the same language:

>>> from gesso.i18n import normalize_lang
>>> normalize_lang("pt_BR.UTF-8")
'pt'
>>> normalize_lang("sr_RS@latin")
'sr'

C and POSIX are not languages

LANG=C means "no locale chosen", not English. Gesso skips such values and keeps looking rather than deciding you asked for English.

Accordingly, normalize_lang returns "" for them — so callers can tell "unspecified" apart from a deliberate fallback — rather than returning a language that was never requested.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text:
A key missing from the selected language falls back to the fallback language, which defaults to English. Translations are merged, not replaced, so a partial translation is a perfectly good translation:

en.jsonfr.json 
{ "myapp": { "menu": { "file": "File", "edit": "Edit" } } }

{ "myapp": { "menu": { "file": "Fichier" } } }

>>> translator.t("myapp.menu.file")
'Fichier'          # from the French catalog
>>> translator.t("myapp.menu.edit")
'Edit'             # missing in French, filled from English

A key missing from every language returns the key itself:

>>> translator.t("myapp.menu.something_new")
'myapp.menu.something_new'

That is deliberate. An empty string is invisible; a dotted key is obviously wrong on screen and greppable in the source, which is what you want while developing. Pass default= when you need something else:

>>> translator.t("myapp.menu.something_new", default="Untitled")
'Untitled'

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
Translations may contain {named} placeholders, filled from keyword arguments:

{ "myapp": { "greeting": "Hello, {name}!" } }

>>> translator.t("myapp.greeting", name="Ada")
'Hello, Ada!'

A malformed placeholder is left as-is rather than raising — one stray brace in a translation file should not prevent the interface from appearing.

docs.title: Direction
docs.text:
>>> from gesso.i18n import is_rtl
>>> is_rtl("ar")
True
>>> is_rtl("en")
False

is_rtl consults a static table rather than pulling in CLDR. It answers the one question a layout actually needs — do I flip the horizontal direction? — and is honest about being nothing more than that.

docs.title: Wiring it into an application
docs.text:
Translator.for_app assembles the three layers for you:

from gesso.i18n import Translator

translator = Translator.for_app(context, locale_dir=Path(__file__).parent / "locales")

print(translator.language)              # 'fr', detected from the environment
print(translator.t("gesso.button.ok"))  # the framework's string
print(translator.t("myapp.menu.file"))  # yours

Changing language at runtime is a reload:

translator.set_language("de")

There is no global translator

Gesso does not keep a process-wide instance, so t("...") never appears in your code as a bare function call. Build a Translator, pass it to the parts of your application that need it, and tests can construct their own.

This is the same reason AppContext is a value you construct rather than a singleton you reach for.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
Two things an internationalisation layer is often expected to do, which Gesso deliberately does not — because doing them properly needs real CLDR data and guessing is worse than waiting:

  • Plural rules. English's one/other split is not how Polish, Arabic or Russian work. Extracting the count-dependent form requires per-language rules.
  • Locale-aware number and date formatting. 1234567.89 is written differently in Germany, India and the United States, and a Monday is not always the first day of the week.

Both are planned as an optional backend rather than a built-in, so the dependency-free core stays dependency-free. See the Roadmap.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
The other half of the design system. The theme tier defines what a card or a segGroup looks like; this tier provides widgets that already call themselves those things.

Every widget sets its own object name. Styling a standard widget never means writing stylesheet — and the object names (card, segGroup, rowLabel, …) are public API, not an implementation detail.

from gesso.ui.widgets import SegmentedControl, SettingRow

control = SegmentedControl([("nasa", "NASA"), ("bing", "Bing")], columns=2)
control.changed.connect(self._provider_chosen)
pane.addWidget(SettingRow(tr("Provider"), control, tr("Which service supplies your wallpaper.")))

docs.title: The set is deliberately small
docs.text:
These are the primitives a settings pane is built from — and each one had a rule already waiting for it in base.qss, which is the honest test of whether something belongs in a library rather than an application:

Widget Object name For Card card A raised surface. Content goes in .body PageHeader pageHeader, pageComment Title, comment, right-aligned actions EmptyState emptyState "Nothing here yet" SettingRow rowLabel, rowDesc Label and description left, control right IconButton iconButton A flat, icon-only button ToggleButton toggleButton An on/off switch SegmentedControl segGroup Mutually exclusive buttons carrying values

Larger composites — a settings explorer, a navigation sidebar, a thumbnail grid — stay in the application until two applications need the same one. Guessing at those here would mean designing an API for a shape nobody has built yet.

docs.title: Two things that are easy to get wrong
Size for the appearance a control will have
docs.text:
A checked ToggleButton and a selected SegmentedControl member are rendered bold by the stylesheet. A button sized from its regular text is truncated the moment it is selected — and a segmented group whose buttons each resize on selection visibly jitters as you use it.

Both widgets therefore measure the bold label up front:

control = SegmentedControl([("a", "Short"), ("b", "A much longer label")])
# every member is the same width, sized to the longest bold label

bold_width() is public, because an application building its own control needs the same guarantee.

docs.title: Loading settings is not a user action
docs.text:
control.set_value("nasa")   # does NOT emit changed
control.buttons[1].click()  # emits changed("bing")

set_value blocks its own signal. Without that, populating a form from stored settings fires the same handler a user's click does — so the application writes back what it just read, re-runs whatever the setting triggers, and in the worst case loops. Qt does not protect you from this, and it is the kind of bug that looks like "the app is slow" rather than "the app is wrong".

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
IconButton takes either a QIcon or an icon name plus a ~gesso.ui.icons.ThemedIcons, so its icon is tinted for the current theme and re-tinted when the theme changes:

from gesso.ui.icons import ThemedIcons

icons = ThemedIcons(theme_manager=themes)
button = IconButton("refresh", icons=icons, role="active", tooltip="Refresh")

Passing a name without an icon set raises rather than silently rendering a blank button.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Working code, not illustrations. Every example is runnable, and each one is exercised by the test suite so it cannot quietly rot.

docs.title: The ladder
docs.text:
The four examples are a ladder. Each rung adds a tier and keeps the one below it, so reading them in order is reading Gesso's feature set in order:

# Example Adds Tiers 1 Hello, Gesso Identity, a schema, all three config formats core, config 2 Basket Constraints, validation, translations, plurals, and data kept apart from settings + i18n 3 Gallery A window: palettes, runtime theme switching, the widget set, icons + ui.theme, ui.icons, ui.widgets 4 Tracker The application shell, pages, a user palette, live language switching + ui.app

Rungs three and four are worth reading as a pair. Gallery builds its own window and lays out its own sidebar by hand. Tracker hands the whole window to AppShell — and Tracker is shorter, despite having four pages, two languages, its own palette, its own icons and a settings file. That difference is the entire argument for the application shell, and it is easier to see in two files than in a paragraph of prose.

docs.title: Running an example
docs.text:
The examples import gesso, which lives under src/. From a checkout:

$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py

The later rungs are packages, so they need examples on the path too:

$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m basket list
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m gallery
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m tracker

Or, with the package installed (pip install -e .):

$ python -m tracker

None of them touch your real ~/.config or ~/.local/share: each takes --config-home and --data-home flags that stand in for $XDG_CONFIG_HOME and $XDG_DATA_HOME.

docs.title: The shape every example follows
docs.text:
Each is deliberately small enough to read in one sitting, and structured the same way:

  1. Who is this application? — an AppSpec.
  2. What does it store? — a Schema.
  3. Let Gesso find the files — ConfigStore.for_app(...).
  4. Do the actual work — the part that is yours.

If you can find those four parts, you can read any of them — and you can see exactly where Gesso stops and the application starts.

docs.title: Basket (CLI)
docs.text:
A grocery list, with settings that are typed and constrained and strings that are not English-only. It is the first rung that could be mistaken for a real program.

Hello, Gesso shows one setting and prints a greeting. Basket adds the two things that make settings hard:

  • some values have to be refused, not merely stored; and
  • a string that reaches the user has to be translatable.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m basket add milk --price 1.20
Added milk. There is 1 item on the list.

$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m basket add bread
Added bread. There are 2 items on the list.

$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m basket list
Shopping list
2 items, sorted by name.

   1. bread
   2. milk                    €1.20

Total: €1.20

$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m basket --language fr list
Liste de courses
2 articles, triés par nom.

   1. bread
   2. milk                    €1.20

Total : €1.20

docs.title: A schema that refuses
docs.text:
The whole specification of what persists:

SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "display",
            title="Display",
            description="How the list is presented.",
            options=(
                Option(
                    "language", str, "auto", "Interface language.",
                    choices=("auto", "en", "fr"),
                ),
                Option("currency", str, "€", "Symbol printed before a price."),
                Option("show_prices", bool, True, "Print a column of prices."),
                Option(
                    "width", int, 24, "Width of the item column, in characters.",
                    minimum=8, maximum=60,
                ),
            ),
        ),
        Section(
            "list",
            title="List",
            description="Rules the list obeys.",
            options=(
                Option(
                    "max_items", int, 50, "Refuse to hold more than this many items.",
                    minimum=1, maximum=500,
                ),
                Option("name_pattern", str, r"^[\w][\w \-']*$", "What an item name may look like."),
            ),
        ),
    ]
)

choices, minimum, maximum and pattern are all constraints, and they are enforced in two places that are easy to confuse:

Where What it does Schema.validate() When you ask Reports everything wrong with the data on disk ConfigStore.set() At the call site Rejects a value, and does not store it

So this does not reach the file:

$ python -m basket config --set list.max_items 9999
error: list.max_items: 9999 exceeds the maximum of 500
$ echo $?
2

9999 is a perfectly good integer. The schema is what refuses it, and the message names the bounds rather than saying "invalid".

docs.title: Coercion is not validation
docs.text:
Those are two different jobs, and the example shows both:

$ python -m basket config --set display.show_prices false
Set display.show_prices to False.

The string "false" was passed on the command line. The schema turned it into a real bool — that is coercion, and it is why getboolean never appears in this codebase. Whether False is a sensible thing for the setting to be is a separate question, and for a boolean it always is.

Both halves live in gesso.config:

  • Option.coerce — make it the declared shape
  • Option.check — say whether that shape is acceptable

docs.title: Settings are not data
docs.text:
Basket keeps two files, and which file is the interesting part:

$ find basket-home -type f | sort
basket-home/basket/config.json
basket-home/basket/items.json
  • The preferences are gesso.config's business: small, typed, and meant to be hand-editable.
  • The shopping list is not. It is a list the user grows, of no fixed shape, so it is plain JSON in the data directory and Gesso stays out of it.

Putting the list in the config file would have been shorter and wrong. That is the distinction AppPaths exists to make: config_dir for what you configure, data_dir for what you accumulate.

There is a third behaviour worth copying:

$ python -m basket list          # reading settings writes nothing
$ ls basket-home/basket/
items.json

A config file appears only once there is something to write into it. Starting an application should not litter.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text:
The catalogs live beside the code, in examples/basket/locales/, and Translator.for_app finds them:

translator = Translator.for_app(
    context,
    language=language or resolve_language(store),
    locale_dir=LOCALES_DIR,
)

Three things are worth knowing about that line.

A stored preference outranks a detected locale — but only when it is set. Basket's language option defaults to "auto", and resolve_language is what that means:

def resolve_language(store: ConfigStore) -> str:
    chosen = store.get("display.language")
    if chosen and chosen != "auto":
        return chosen
    return detect_language() or DEFAULT_LANGUAGE

Gesso will not guess this for you. A stored preference outranking the system locale is one possible policy; so is the opposite. Only the application knows whether its setting means "unset" or means a literal value.

The search order goes from the framework out to the user. In ascending priority: Gesso's own catalogs, then the application's, then a directory beside the user's settings. So a user can override any string without touching the application:

$ cat basket-home/basket/i18n/fr.json
{ "basket": { "list": { "heading": "Ma liste" } } }

Plural forms are the application's job, and Basket does them by hand:

def plural(t, key, count, **kwargs) -> str:
    form = "one" if count == 1 else "other"
    return t(f"{key}.{form}", count=count, **kwargs)

That is not laziness. Plural rules are not one-versus-many in most languages — Russian has three forms, Arabic six — and getting them right needs real CLDR data, which Gesso's roadmap lists as an optional backend rather than pretending to have. For English and French the rule really is this simple, so the catalogs carry both forms and the application chooses.

A missing translation does not fail

It prints English. Nothing raises, no test turns red, and the bug ships. Basket's suite catches it by comparing the two catalogs key-for-key:

def test_the_catalogs_cover_the_same_keys():
    assert keys_of(load_catalog("en")) == keys_of(load_catalog("fr"))

If you take one test from this example, take that one.

docs.title: One flag is not the other
docs.text:
$ python -m basket --language fr list     # this run only
$ python -m basket config --set display.language fr   # remembered

--language is a top-level flag meaning "for this run". To change the setting you go through config --set like every other setting — which means it is coerced, checked and reported by the same machinery as everything else.

This was not the first design. basket config --language fr looks natural and cannot work: argparse will not route a top-level flag into a subcommand. The flag was given a meaning that matches what it can actually do.

docs.title: What it demonstrates
docs.text:
• Constraints that reject at set() and report at validate()
  • Coercion separated from validation
  • Configuration and application data, in the right directories
  • Reading settings without creating a file
  • A translator that searches framework → application → user
  • Plural forms chosen by the application, and why Gesso does not guess them
  • A catalog-completeness test, which is the only cheap way to catch a missing string

docs.title: Gallery (GUI)
docs.text:
The first example with a window, and the last one that builds its own layout. It puts the design system on screen — every palette, every widget, every icon role and every design token — and lets you switch themes underneath them.

It is also a tool you can leave open. When a widget looks wrong, Gallery is where you find out whether the fault is the palette, the stylesheet or your own code.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m gallery
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m gallery --theme light
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m gallery --list-themes
dark
light

The window has a palette switcher at the top and five cards below it: buttons, rows, an empty state, an icon matrix, and the token inspector.

docs.title: Nothing styles itself
docs.text:
This is the point of the example. Every widget Gesso ships sets its own object name, and the base stylesheet matches on it. The application writes no QSS at all:

card = Card(margins=20, spacing=14)
card.body.addWidget(section_title("Buttons"))

Card sets objectName("card"). A heading set up like this:

def section_title(text: str) -> QLabel:
    label = QLabel(text)
    label.setObjectName("sectionTitle")
    return label

...is styled by the same rule the application shell's page headers use, because they agree on the same name.

Those object names — card, rowLabel, segGroup, emptyState — are the public contract between the widget library and the stylesheet. They are also deliberately unqualified: the stylesheet says #card, not QFrame#card, so a QLabel can be a card if you want one to be.

The one place an inline stylesheet is right

The token inspector draws a colour swatch per token, and it sets a stylesheet string to do it:

swatch.setStyleSheet(f"background-color: {value}; border-radius: 3px;")

That looks like exactly the thing the design system tells you not to do. It is not: this colour is data read out of the palette at runtime. There is no object name that could express "whatever this token currently is", and hard-coding a name would defeat the point of inspecting it.

The rule is "no style rules in the application" — not "no stylesheets".

docs.title: Switching palettes
docs.text:
ThemeManager does three things on apply(name), and the third is the one people forget:

def apply_theme(self, name: str) -> bool:
    self.manager.apply(name)
    self._render_tokens()
    applied = self.manager.current.name if self.manager.current else None
    if applied is not None:
        self.theme_control.set_value(applied)
    ...
  1. the stylesheet is re-rendered from the new palette's tokens;
  2. the QPalette is rebuilt, so natively-drawn furniture — tooltips, menu shadows, text selection — matches instead of falling back to the platform default;
  3. and the application repaints whatever a theme change staled.

That last one is the application's job, because Gesso cannot know what your widgets are holding. Which brings us to icons.

docs.title: Icons do not repaint themselves
docs.text:
An icon is rendered into a QPixmap and tinted. A QLabel holds that pixmap. A pixmap does not know the theme moved, so nothing happens unless something rebuilds it:

self.icons.iconsChanged.connect(self._refresh_icons)

ThemedIcons emits iconsChanged after a theme change. It says when; you decide what. Gallery keeps the role each button was built for and re-renders the matrix:

def _refresh_icons(self) -> None:
    self._render_icons()
    for button, role in self._role_buttons:
        button.set_role(role)

The roles are worth knowing, because they are tokens rather than colours:

Role Token For idle text_muted a resting icon strong text one that should stand out active accent selected disabled text_disabled unavailable on-accent accent_text sitting on an accent-coloured surface

Because each role names a token, one piece of artwork is correct in every theme. Adding a theme never means adding a second copy of the icons.

docs.title: The token inspector
docs.text:
The bottom card lists all thirty tokens, their group, and what each resolves to in the current palette. It is the fastest way to answer "why is this the wrong grey?".

It also shows something worth understanding about how palettes work: a palette may be partial. Anything it leaves out falls back to the contract's last-resort default, which is why a palette only has to state what it wants to change. Tracker ships one that does exactly that.

docs.title: A fallback that is not a failure
docs.text:
Gallery's apply_theme returns whether the palette you asked for is the one in force — which is not the same question as whether apply succeeded:

$ # a palette with no file installed
>>> window.apply_theme("chartreuse")
False
>>> window.manager.current.name
'dark'

ThemeManager.apply falls back rather than failing. A user who deletes a theme file should get the application's own look, not a neutral window nobody chose. So apply returns True — something was applied — and only the caller can tell the difference between "worked" and "worked, but not as asked".

That is a deliberate design, and it is the kind of thing that is much easier to copy from a working example than to infer from an API listing.

docs.title: Hello, Gesso (CLI)
docs.text: A complete command-line application in one file. It stores a greeting the way you tell it to, in any of the three supported formats, and it is short enough to read in a few minutes.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py
Hello, World!

$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py --set greeting.name Ada
Hello, Ada!

$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py --show
{
  "greeting": {
    "name": "Ada",
    "punctuation": "!",
    "shout": false,
    "repeat": 1
  }
}

docs.title: The whole program
docs.text:
"""A complete, runnable Gesso application — in a single file.

Gesso's whole job is to get out of the way, so this example is deliberately
small. It declares *who the application is* (an :class:`~gesso.core.AppSpec`),
*what it stores* (a :class:`~gesso.config.Schema`), and lets Gesso work out
*where* that lives and *in what format*.

Try it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py --set greeting.name Ada
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py --format toml --show
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/hello.py --convert yaml

``--config-home`` stands in for ``$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`` and defaults to
``./hello-config``, so the example never touches your real ``~/.config``. Note
where the files actually land — Gesso nests them under the application id::

    hello-config/
    └── gesso-hello/
        └── config.json
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Optional

from gesso.config import ConfigError, ConfigStore, Option, Schema, Section
from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec
from gesso.core.paths import AppPaths

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Who is this application?
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
APP = AppSpec(
    name="Gesso Hello",
    app_id="gesso-hello",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="A tiny example application built on Gesso.",
    default_config_format="json",
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. What does it store?
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "greeting",
            title="Greeting",
            description="How the application greets you.",
            options=(
                Option("name", str, "World", "Who to greet."),
                Option("punctuation", str, "!", "Appended to the greeting."),
                Option("shout", bool, False, "Print the greeting in UPPERCASE."),
                Option("repeat", int, 1, "How many times to print the greeting."),
            ),
        )
    ]
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Let Gesso find (or plan) the configuration file.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def build_store(config_home: Path, fmt: Optional[str]) -> ConfigStore:
    """Locate this application's configuration, in *fmt* if one is forced."""
    context = AppContext(APP, AppPaths.resolve(APP.app_id, config_home=config_home))
    if fmt:
        return ConfigStore.for_format(SCHEMA, context.config_dir, fmt).load()
    return ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, context).load()


def render(store: ConfigStore) -> str:
    """Turn the stored settings into the greeting to print."""
    text = f"Hello, {store.get('greeting.name')}{store.get('greeting.punctuation')}"
    if store.get("greeting.shout"):
        text = text.upper()
    return "\n".join([text] * store.get("greeting.repeat"))


def main(argv: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="hello", description="A tiny application built on Gesso."
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--config-home",
        type=Path,
        default=Path("hello-config"),
        help="Stands in for $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default: ./hello-config)",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--format",
        choices=("json", "toml", "yaml"),
        help="Force a configuration format instead of discovering one",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--set",
        nargs=2,
        action="append",
        default=[],
        metavar=("KEY", "VALUE"),
        help="Set a value, e.g. --set greeting.name Ada",
    )
    parser.add_argument("--show", action="store_true", help="Print the configuration and exit")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--convert", metavar="FORMAT", help="Rewrite the configuration in another format"
    )
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    try:
        store = build_store(args.config_home, args.format)
    except ConfigError as exc:
        print(f"error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    for key, value in args.set:
        try:
            store.set(key, value)
        except ConfigError as exc:
            print(f"error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
            return 2
    if args.set:
        store.save()

    for problem in store.validate():
        print(f"warning: {problem}", file=sys.stderr)

    if args.convert:
        try:
            store.convert_to(args.convert)
        except ConfigError as exc:
            print(f"error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
            return 2

    if args.show:
        print(json.dumps(store.as_dict(), indent=2))
    else:
        print(render(store))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text: The file is in four parts, and the first three are the ones Gesso cares about.

docs.title: 1. Who is this application?
docs.text:
APP = AppSpec(
    name="Gesso Hello",
    app_id="gesso-hello",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="A tiny example application built on Gesso.",
    default_config_format="json",
)

Three of these fields do real work:

  • app_id becomes the directory name — gesso-hello/config.json.
  • default_config_format decides what is created on first run.
  • version and description are what a future About box, QSettings organisation, or systemd unit will read, so that none of them has to be maintained separately.

docs.title: 2. What does it store?
docs.text:
SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "greeting",
            ...
            options=(
                Option("name", str, "World", "Who to greet."),
                Option("punctuation", str, "!", "Appended to the greeting."),
                Option("shout", bool, False, "Print the greeting in UPPERCASE."),
                Option("repeat", int, 1, "How many times to print the greeting."),
            ),
        )
    ]
)

This is the entire specification of what persists: two strings, a boolean and an integer, each with a default. No getboolean, no int(...), no "true".

docs.title: 3. Let Gesso find the file
docs.text:
def build_store(config_home: Path, fmt: Optional[str]) -> ConfigStore:
    """Locate this application's configuration, in *fmt* if one is forced."""
    context = AppContext(APP, AppPaths.resolve(APP.app_id, config_home=config_home))
    if fmt:
        return ConfigStore.for_format(SCHEMA, context.config_dir, fmt).load()
    return ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, context).load()

The one line worth pausing on is AppPaths.resolve(APP.app_id, config_home=...). --config-home stands in for $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, which is what keeps the example from writing into your real ~/.config — and, more importantly, it is the same mechanism that lets the test suite run without side effects.

Note what is not here: no Path.home(), no "gesso-hello" string in a path, no format table. Those all come from the AppSpec and the schema.

docs.title: 4. Do the actual work
docs.text:
def render(store: ConfigStore) -> str:
    """Turn the stored settings into the greeting to print."""
    text = f"Hello, {store.get('greeting.name')}{store.get('greeting.punctuation')}"
    if store.get("greeting.shout"):
        text = text.upper()
    return "\n".join([text] * store.get("greeting.repeat"))

Everything above this is plumbing Gesso provides. This function is the application.

docs.title: main: wiring it up
docs.text:
main is ordinary argparse, with a few calls into the store:

Flag What it does --config-home PATH Where $XDG_CONFIG_HOME would be --format {json,toml,yaml} Force a format instead of discovering one --set KEY VALUE Set a value, coerced by the schema --show Print the whole configuration as JSON --convert FORMAT Rewrite the configuration in another format

Two behaviours are worth copying:

for problem in store.validate():
    print(f"warning: {problem}", file=sys.stderr)

Problems are reported, not fatal — the application still starts. And:

except ConfigError as exc:
    print(f"error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
    return 2

Every failure path prints a message that names the actual problem and exits non-zero, rather than raising a traceback at the user.

docs.title: Play with the formats
docs.text:
JSON (default)YAMLTOML 
$ python examples/hello.py --set greeting.name Ada
$ cat hello-config/gesso-hello/config.json

{
  "greeting": {
    "name": "Ada",
    "punctuation": "!",
    "shout": false,
    "repeat": 1
  }
}

$ python examples/hello.py --format yaml --set greeting.name Ada
$ cat hello-config/gesso-hello/config.yaml

greeting:
  name: Ada
  punctuation: '!'
  shout: false
  repeat: 1

$ python examples/hello.py --format toml --set greeting.name Ada

Requires gesso-sdk[toml]. Without it you get a message naming the package to install, not an obscure failure.

docs.title: Convert between formats
docs.text:
$ python examples/hello.py --convert yaml
$ ls hello-config/gesso-hello/
config.json.bak  config.yaml

The old file is kept as a .bak, and the values come across intact — including their types.

docs.title: Try to break it
docs.text:
$ python examples/hello.py --set greeting.repeat lots
error: greeting.repeat: cannot read 'lots' as an integer

The value is rejected at the call site. It never reaches the file, and the user gets a sentence instead of a stack trace.

docs.title: Tracker (GUI)
docs.text:
The top of the ladder: every tier in one small application. Typed settings, a habit log kept apart from them, two languages with plural forms, a palette of its own, its own icons, and four pages assembled by the application shell.

It is also the shortest of the three GUI examples to read — and that is the point.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m tracker
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m tracker --language fr
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m tracker --theme light
$ PYTHONPATH=src:examples python -m tracker --config-home ./tracker-home

It opens on Today — a toggle per habit, a progress line, and a streak under each habit. History lists the last seven days. Settings is every setting. About says where the two files live.

docs.title: Compare it with Gallery
docs.text:
This is the most useful thing to do with this example.

Gallery builds its own window. It creates a QMainWindow, a central widget, a root layout, a sidebar frame, a brand label, a navigation column, a button group, a scroll area and a page stack — roughly 130 lines of chrome before it does anything of its own.

Tracker does this instead:

for key, label, comment, icon in PAGES:
    page = pages[key]
    shell.add_page(
        key,
        session.t(label),
        page,
        comment=session.t(comment) if comment else "",
        icon=icon,
        actions=page.header_actions(),
    )

Ten lines. Tracker has four pages, two languages, its own palette, its own icons and a settings file — and it is shorter than Gallery, which has one page and none of those.

add_page is doing the work: it wraps the page in a header, builds a navigation entry for it, keeps the two in step, and adds it to the stack. The page never learns where its buttons ended up.

docs.title: A page is just a widget
docs.text:
Tracker's pages share a tiny base class:

class Page(QWidget):
    def header_actions(self) -> List[QWidget]:
        """Buttons for the header row. Default: none."""
        return []

    def retranslate(self) -> None:
        """Say everything again, in whatever language is now active."""

Both hooks are optional, and neither is a Gesso type. A page is a QWidget; these are just the two questions the application asks of one. Adding a fifth page means writing a widget.

docs.title: The shell speaks your language
docs.text:
Gesso's shell has strings of its own. It does not ship them in English and leave you to live with it — it looks them up through your translator, under a reserved gesso. domain:

return run_app(
    APP,
    lambda shell: build(shell, session),
    ...
    translate=session.t,
)

So when Tracker switches to French, the drawer button's tooltip changes too:

>>> shell.drawer_button.toolTip()
'Show or hide the navigation'
>>> # ...switch to French...
>>> shell.drawer_button.toolTip()
'Afficher ou masquer la navigation'

That is the reserved domain earning its keep. The framework owns gesso.*, the application owns everything else, and the two cannot collide. A missing translation shows the raw key rather than an empty string, so you can see it on screen and grep for it in the source.

docs.title: Changing language without restarting
docs.text:
A page's title lives in three places — the Page record, the navigation button, and the header. Retitling two of them is worse than retitling none, so the shell does all three at once:

shell.set_page_title(key, session.t(label), session.t(comment))

...and re-says its own strings:

shell.retranslate()

Both of these exist because Tracker needed them. That is worth noticing: a framework grows its API from the applications that use it, not from design sessions.

docs.title: A palette of its own
docs.text:
Tracker ships examples/tracker/themes/midnight.json, and it is deliberately partial — sixteen tokens out of thirty:

{
  "name": "Midnight",
  "description": "Tracker's own palette. Deliberately partial: the contract supplies anything a palette leaves out...",
  "colors": {
    "window": "#15161e",
    "panel": "#1b1d27",
    "card": "#22242f",
    "text_strong": "#eef1ff",
    "accent": "#7aa2f7"
  }
}

The fourteen it omits are not missing. The token contract has a last-resort default for every token, so a palette only has to state what it wants to change. ThemeManager.problems("midnight") returns nothing, and the scrollbars still work.

builtin_theme_dirs replaces; icon_dirs appends

These two arguments look like a pair and behave differently:

builtin_theme_dirs=[THEMES_DIR, BUILTIN_PALETTES_DIR],
icon_dirs=[ICONS_DIR],

Passing only [THEMES_DIR] gives you Midnight and loses dark and light. This is deliberate — Gesso's stylesheet references Gesso's icon names, so those directories must stay resolvable, whereas nothing breaks if a palette is absent — but it surprises people. An application that wants its own palette and Gesso's names both.

docs.title: Icons from two places, one registry
docs.text:
Tracker ships two icons — a chart and a set of sliders — and uses two of Gesso's:

PAGES = (
    ("today", "tracker.nav.today", "tracker.page.today", "check"),
    ("history", "tracker.nav.history", "tracker.page.history", "streak"),
    ("settings", "tracker.nav.settings", "tracker.page.settings", "settings"),
    ("about", "tracker.nav.about", "", "info"),
)

All four resolve, because Tracker's directory is appended to Gesso's rather than substituted for it. That is what makes icon_dirs an append: the stylesheet's spin-box arrows are addressed by name from Gesso's directory, so replacing the search path would leave them unresolved.

docs.title: Settings, and the data next to them
docs.text:
The schema is ordinary — choices, bounds, defaults:

Section(
    "display",
    title="Display",
    description="How the window looks and reads.",
    options=(
        Option("language", str, "auto", "Interface language. 'auto' follows your system locale.",
               choices=("auto", "en", "fr")),
        Option("theme", str, "midnight", "Palette to use."),
        Option("show_streaks", bool, True, "Show how many days in a row each habit runs."),
        ...
    ),
)

Two things about it are worth noting.

No choices for the theme. The valid palettes are whichever ones Gesso can find — Midnight, plus Gesso's, plus whatever the user dropped into ~/.config/tracker/themes/. A schema listing them would be wrong the moment a user added one, so it constrains what it can and stays out of the rest.

The habits are not in here. They live in tracker.json in the data directory, as plain Python. A schema is for settings: small, typed, and meant to be hand-edited. A list the user grows is none of those things.

Moving to auto also does not freeze today's answer:

def set_language(self, language: str, *, persist: bool = True) -> str:
    chosen = language or "auto"
    resolved = chosen if chosen != "auto" else (detect_language() or DEFAULT_LANGUAGE)
    ...
    if persist:
        self.store.set("display.language", chosen)

Picking "System" stores auto, so the preference keeps meaning "whatever my machine says" rather than becoming a snapshot of this afternoon's locale.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Version Notes Python 3.9 or newer 3.11+ gives you TOML reading from the standard library PySide6 6.5 or newer Only needed for the Qt layer (gesso.ui)

Gesso's core has no runtime dependencies at all.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install gesso-sdk

That gives you gesso.core and gesso.config with JSON support.

Why isn't the package called gesso?

The distribution is named gesso-sdk because the name gesso on PyPI is held by an unrelated, dormant project, as are gesso on crates.io (a Rust Wayland wallpaper daemon) and npm (an Acro Media design system).

The import name is gesso — import gesso is what you write in code.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Each heavier capability is opt-in, so a command-line tool never drags in Qt.

TOMLYAMLQt interfaceEverything

Needed both to read and to write TOML. On Python 3.11+ reading uses the standard library, but writing always needs tomli-w.

pip install "gesso-sdk[toml]"

pip install "gesso-sdk[yaml]"

pip install "gesso-sdk[gui]"

pip install "gesso-sdk[toml,yaml,gui]"

A missing extra is never a surprise

If a configuration file exists in a format whose backend is not installed, Gesso tells you exactly what to install rather than failing obscurely:

error: found /home/you/.config/myapp/config.toml but writing TOML requires
the 'tomli-w' package (pip install 'gesso-sdk[toml]')

What it will not do is quietly create a second configuration file in a different format next to the one it could not read.
