docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Five minutes, one file, a working application that remembers its settings — in whichever format you prefer.

docs.title: The fast way: gesso new
docs.text:
pip install -e /path/to/gesso        # Gesso is not on PyPI yet
gesso new myapp
cd myapp
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest
python -m myapp.main

That writes a working application — config schema, palette, translations, a window and a passing test — so you start from something that runs rather than an empty directory. See the generator for what is in it.

The rest of this page builds the same foundations by hand, which is worth reading if you want to know what the scaffold is doing.

docs.title: 1. Write the application
docs.text:
Save this as myapp.py:

from gesso.config import ConfigStore, Option, Schema, Section
from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec

# Who is this application?
APP = AppSpec("My App", app_id="myapp")

# What does it store?
SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "editor",
            options=(
                Option("font_size", int, 13, "Editor font size in points."),
                Option("wrap", bool, True, "Wrap long lines."),
                Option("theme", str, "dark", "Colour scheme."),
            ),
        )
    ]
)


def main() -> None:
    context = AppContext(APP)
    store = ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, context).load()

    print("font size:", store.get("editor.font_size"))
    print("wrap     :", store.get("editor.wrap"))

    # `set` takes whatever you give it and coerces to the declared type.
    store.set("editor.font_size", "15")  # a string in, an int out
    print("after set:", store.get("editor.font_size"), end=" ")
    print(f"({type(store.get('editor.font_size')).__name__})")

    store.save()
    print("saved to :", store.path)


main()

docs.title: 2. Run it
docs.text:
$ python myapp.py
font size: 13
wrap     : True
after set: 15 (<class 'int'>)
saved to : /home/you/.config/myapp/config.json

That last line is the interesting one. You never said where to put the configuration or what format to use — Gesso derived both. The directory comes from app_id placed under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, and the format from the application's default_config_format.

docs.title: 3. Look at what it wrote
docs.text:
$ cat ~/.config/myapp/config.json

{
  "editor": {
    "font_size": 15,
    "wrap": true,
    "theme": "dark"
  }
}

Notice font_size is the number 15 and wrap is a real boolean — not "15" and "true". That is the schema doing its job. A configuration whose values are all strings cannot survive contact with TOML, and produces a steady stream of bugs long before that.

docs.title: 4. Change the format
docs.text:
The format is a property of the file, not of its contents, so switching is just a different extension. Copy the same file and change one line:

store = ConfigStore.for_format(SCHEMA, context.config_dir, "yaml").load()

$ python myapp.py
$ cat ~/.config/myapp/config.yaml

editor:
  font_size: 15
  wrap: true
  theme: dark

Or convert an existing configuration in place:

store.convert_to("toml")   # writes config.toml, keeps config.yaml.bak

TOML needs an extra

TOML writing requires tomli-w. Without it, Gesso raises a clear error naming the package to install rather than failing obscurely. See Installation.

docs.title: 5. See the whole example
docs.text: myapp.py above is the short version. The examples/hello.py walkthrough builds the same idea into a complete command-line application with argument parsing, --set, --show and --convert.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Understand the design — Architecture
  • Learn the identity layer — Application identity
  • Go deep on configuration — Configuration

docs.title: Choosing a config format
docs.text: Gesso supports JSON, TOML and YAML as first-class formats. Which one is in use is a property of the file — decided by its extension — never something recorded inside the file itself.

docs.title: Why not store the format in the file?
docs.text:
Because it is circular. A configuration file cannot reliably tell you how to parse it, since you must parse it to find out. Every scheme that tries — a magic comment, a format: key, a .configrc pointer — needs a bootstrap rule anyway, and then you have two sources of truth that can disagree.

Making the extension authoritative means:

  • cat ~/.config/myapp/config.toml — you know what you are looking at.
  • Every existing tool on the system (git, $EDITOR, yq, schema validators) already works.
  • Converting is a file rename plus a re-serialise.

docs.title: How the format is resolved
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S([ConfigStore.discover]) --> A{Explicit path?}
    A -- yes --> B[The suffix picks the codec]
    A -- no --> C["Scan the config directory for<br/>config.json / config.toml<br/>config.yaml / config.yml"]
    C --> D{How many found?}
    D -- "exactly one" --> E[Use it]
    D -- "more than one" --> F["Use the preferred one and<br/>report the rest as ambiguous"]
    D -- none --> G["Plan to create the<br/>preferred format"]
    B --> H([Ready to load])
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
Step Detail 1. Explicit path ConfigStore.for_path() — the suffix decides, and an unrecognised suffix is an error 2. Discover ConfigStore.discover() — first match wins, in a documented precedence order 3. Ambiguity More than one config file is reported, in store.others, never silently guessed at 4. First run No file yet — the store is bound to the preferred format and writes it on the first save()

The failure mode this prevents

Silently creating a second configuration file next to one you could not read is how an application ends up with two live configs that disagree — the user edits one, the program reads the other. Gesso refuses:

error: found /home/you/.config/myapp/config.toml but writing TOML requires
the 'tomli-w' package (pip install 'gesso-sdk[toml]')

docs.title: The three codecs compared
docs.text:
JSON TOML YAML Dependency none (stdlib) tomli/tomllib + tomli-w PyYAML Comments none yes yes Native types yes yes yes Hand-editable acceptable excellent good Round-trip comments — lost by tomli-w lost by PyYAML Ambiguity risk none none no → False, and more Best for defaults, machine-written hand-edited settings data-shaped configs

Choose JSON as the default: zero dependencies, no ambiguity, and machine round-trips it perfectly. Offer TOML to users who want comments in a file they edit by hand. Offer YAML when the configuration is genuinely data-shaped.

YAML is the loosest of the three

PyYAML's safe_load decodes unquoted no as False. That is correct YAML, and surprising to nearly everyone. Gesso only ever uses safe_load (never load, which can construct arbitrary Python objects), and the typed schema is what stops the looseness reaching your application — but it is a good reason not to reach for YAML by reflex.

docs.title: Letting the user choose
docs.text:
Offer the choice through your own interface, and pass it straight through. Notice that the third line is the entire implementation:

# fmt is whatever the user picked: "json", "toml" or "yaml"
store = ConfigStore.for_format(SCHEMA, context.config_dir, fmt).load()

To offer "use whatever is already there, else this format", use discovery instead — it takes the fallback as a parameter:

store = ConfigStore.discover(SCHEMA, context.config_dir, preferred="toml")
if store.others:
    warn("several config files found; using %s and ignoring %s" % (store.path, store.others))

docs.title: Converting
docs.text:
new_path = store.convert_to("toml")   # writes config.toml

convert_to reads through the current codec and writes through the target one. It is deliberately cautious:

  • The previous file is kept as config.<old>.bak unless you pass keep_backup=False.
  • It refuses to overwrite an existing file of the target format, rather than destroying one of the two configurations.
  • Converting to the format you are already using is a no-op.

docs.title: A word on secrets
docs.text:
Whatever format you choose, keep credentials out of the configuration file. A user who picks YAML because they want to read and share it is exactly the user who will paste an API key into version control.

Gesso's recommendation: keep non-secret preferences in the config, and put secrets in the platform keyring, or a separate file with 0600 permissions. The config is for settings, not for credentials.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Defining a schema

docs.title: Defining a schema
docs.text: A schema is the contract between your application and its configuration file: every setting, its type, its default, and what it means.

docs.title: A complete schema
docs.text:
from gesso.config import Option, Schema, Section

SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "editor",
            title="Editor",
            description="How text is displayed and edited.",
            options=(
                Option("font_size", int, 13, "Font size, in points."),
                Option("font_family", str, "monospace", "The font to use."),
                Option("wrap", bool, True, "Wrap long lines."),
                Option("tab_width", int, 4, "Spaces per tab stop."),
            ),
        ),
        Section(
            "files",
            title="Files",
            description="Where files are opened from and saved to.",
            options=(
                Option("last_dir", str, "~/Documents", "Directory to open on startup."),
                Option("autosave", bool, False, "Save automatically while typing."),
                Option("recent", list, [], "Recently opened files."),
            ),
        ),
    ]
)

That is the whole thing. It reads as documentation because it is the documentation — the description on each option is what a future settings window, or a generated reference, will show.

docs.title: The three objects
docs.text:
OptionSectionSchema

One setting.

Parameter Meaning key The name within its section, e.g. font_size type bool, int, float, str, list or dict default Used when the key is absent from the file description Human-readable help

A named group of options — one table in JSON/TOML/YAML.

Parameter Meaning name The table name, e.g. editor options A tuple of Options title Display name, for a settings UI description What the section covers

The ordered collection of sections. Ordered because presentation order is meaningful in a settings window, and dicts would make it arbitrary.

docs.title: Naming sections
docs.text:
Reuse your own vocabulary, and prefer a small number of meaningful sections over one flat namespace. editor.font_size reads better at a call site than font_size, and it gives a settings UI something to group by:

store.get("editor.font_size")
store.get("files.last_dir")

docs.title: Defaults are the migration mechanism
docs.text:
Because a missing key is filled from the schema default, a configuration file never has to be complete. Users can write the two settings they care about and ignore the rest:

{ "editor": { "font_size": 15 } }

and your application still reads a fully-populated configuration. This is also how you add a setting without breaking anyone:

  1. Add the Option to your schema.
  2. Ship the release.

Every existing file picks up the default on next load. There is no migration to write, and no version gate to add. See Validating and migrating for when that stops being enough.

docs.title: Keep the schema in one place
docs.text:
Give the schema a name and import it, rather than rebuilding it where it is needed — a schema built twice is a schema that will drift:

# myapp/config.py
SCHEMA = Schema([...])

# anywhere else
from myapp.config import SCHEMA

docs.title: What not to put in the schema
docs.text:
• Secrets. API keys and tokens belong in the keyring (see Choosing a config format).
  • Derived state. Anything you can recompute — a cache directory, a resolved absolute path — is not a setting.
  • Per-run values. A schema describes persistence. If it should not survive a restart, it is not configuration.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Validating and migrating

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
validate() returns a list of human-readable problems. An empty list means valid.

for problem in store.validate():
    print("warning:", problem)

warning: unknown section [generl]
warning: unknown option editor.font_sizee
warning: editor.tab_width: cannot read 'wide' as an integer

Each message names the exact key, so a user can fix the file without reading your source.

docs.title: What counts as a problem
docs.text:
Situation Problem? Why Unknown section or key Yes Almost always a typo, and silently ignoring it hides the user's intent Value that will not coerce Yes The application would otherwise get the wrong type or crash later A section that is not a table Yes Structurally wrong, not merely surprising A missing key No Filled from the schema default — see below A value of the right type No —

Validation is advisory, not fatal

validate() never raises and never mutates. It is up to you whether a problem is a warning in a log, a banner in the UI, or a refusal to start. Gesso's own example prints warnings and carries on, which is the right default: a malformed preference should not stop a user opening their application.

docs.title: Loading never destroys data
docs.text:
This is a guarantee, not a side effect. When Gesso loads a file it preserves keys it does not recognise, and values it cannot coerce, rather than pruning them.

>>> store.get("editor.mystery")     # not in the schema
7
>>> store.validate()
['unknown option editor.mystery']

Why this matters: if loading silently dropped unknown keys, then one run of a newer version followed by an older version would quietly delete the user's settings. A configuration file belongs to the user. Gesso reads it, reports on it, and writes back only what it was given or told to change.

docs.title: Adding a setting
docs.text:
You almost certainly do not need to do anything. Add the Option to your schema and ship:

Option("show_line_numbers", bool, True, "Display line numbers.")

Existing files gain the default on next load. This covers the large majority of real-world configuration changes, and it is why the schema exists.

docs.title: Renaming or restructuring
docs.text:
When a key moves or changes meaning, a default cannot express the intent — you need to carry the old value forward. Do that explicitly, right after loading:

store = ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, context).load()

# Migration: `tab_size` was renamed to `tab_width` in 2.0.
legacy = store.get("editor.tab_size")
if legacy is not None:
    store.set("editor.tab_width", legacy)
    store.save()

Guiding principles:

  • Migrate forward only. Do not write downgrade paths; they are rarely correct and never tested.
  • Be idempotent. The check above is a no-op once the old key is gone, so it is safe to run on every startup.
  • Never fail to start over a migration. If you cannot carry a value across, fall back to the default and warn — losing one preference is better than losing the application.

Schema-version migrations are not built yet

A declarative migration framework — a schema version plus an ordered list of upgrade steps, applied automatically on load — is on the roadmap. Today, migrations are explicit code like the example above, which is honest and adequate for a young application. If you need version tracking now, store it yourself as a normal option:

Option("config_version", int, 1, "Schema version, for migrations.")

class Option:
    key: str
    type: type
    default: Any
    description: str = ""

Method Description coerce(value) Convert to the declared type; raises ValueError on failure check(value) Constraint problems with an already-coerced value; empty means acceptable coerce_and_check(value) Both, returning (value, problems)

Type and constraint are separate concerns. A type says what shape a value is; a constraint says whether that value is acceptable. "nonsense" fails the type; 99999 passes the type but fails the constraint.

docs.text:
Scaffolding a new project. No Qt needed — the generator writes files.

docs.title: The gesso command
docs.text:
gesso new PATH [--name NAME] [--app-id ID] [--org ORG] [--description TEXT] [--overwrite]
gesso --version

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
myapp/
├── pyproject.toml          # packaging, entry point, pytest config
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── src/myapp/
│   ├── app.py              # the AppSpec, context and translator
│   ├── config.py           # the settings schema
│   ├── home.py             # a page
│   ├── main.py             # run_app, and `build`
│   ├── locales/en.json
│   └── themes/default.json
└── tests/
    ├── conftest.py         # Qt on the offscreen platform
    └── test_app.py

create(spec, "myapp")                # or write it

docs.title: Writing a template
docs.text:
Templates live in gesso/templates/ and are rendered with string.Template:

Placeholder Value ${name} The display name ${app_id} The application id, e.g. my-app ${package} The Python package, e.g. my_app ${org} The organisation ${version} The version ${description} The description ${year} The current year

A destination may contain a placeholder too — that is how one template tree lands in a package named after the application.

A literal dollar sign must be doubled

docs.title: seed_user_dir
docs.text: A user cannot edit a theme they cannot see, so seeding makes the shipped palettes discoverable. Copies are only written where nothing exists unless overwrite is set, which means an edit is never clobbered — and a later release of an application cannot silently undo a user's customisation. Failures are ignored: a read-only config directory costs the user their copies, not the application.

docs.title: apply
docs.text:
Sets the stylesheet and the palette, and emits themeChanged when the theme actually changes. A name with no palette installed falls back to the default theme, so a user whose theme file was deleted gets the application's own look rather than a neutral one.

Returns False — rather than raising — when there is no application to style or the stylesheet cannot be rendered: a theme is a preference, and a broken one should not stop an application opening.

Re-applying the same theme does not re-emit. Widgets re-tint on a change, and a redundant signal would make every application redraw for nothing.

docs.title: palette
docs.text: Qt draws tooltips, menu frames and other native furniture from the QPalette, not from the stylesheet. Setting only the stylesheet leaves those at the platform default, which is how a themed application ends up with a yellow tooltip.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Short, hands-on walkthroughs. Each one covers one tier, is self-contained, and ends with something you can run.

They are not a course: you do not have to read them in order, and none of them assumes you have read the others. If you are starting from nothing, read Configuration first, then pick whichever tier you need.

docs.title: The tutorials
docs.text: Tutorial You end up with Needs Qt Store a setting A schema that types and refuses values no Translate an application Two catalogs, plurals, and a user override no Make a palette A partial palette and a rendered stylesheet no Ship your own icons Your artwork, tinted by the theme yes Build a settings pane A pane with no stylesheet of its own yes Build a windowed application Two pages, a status line, one call yes

docs.title: Every tutorial is a real file
docs.text:
The code in these pages is not written for the page. Each tutorial is an actual script under examples/tutorials/, and the pages embed it with --8<-- so the two cannot drift. The suite runs each one as a subprocess, using the same command line the page gives you.

So if a tutorial is wrong, a test is red.

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
From a checkout:

$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/settings.py

The Qt ones need a display, or a way to pretend:

$ PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/pane.py
$ QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/pane.py --check

--check builds everything and closes immediately instead of entering the event loop. That is what CI uses, and it is a good habit for your own applications.

Where you are told to look, and why

Each tutorial explains not only what to write but why the API is shaped the way it is — because in every case there was a plausible alternative that turned out worse. Those notes are the most useful part of a tutorial and the easiest thing to leave out.

docs.title: After the tutorials
docs.text:
• The examples — the same tiers, in applications rather than in isolation, building from a CLI up to a full GUI.
  • Concepts — the reasoning behind the layering.
  • Guides — how to decide, rather than how to do.

docs.title: Store a setting
docs.text:
You will end up with a settings file that types itself, refuses values it should not hold, and can be rewritten in another format.

No Qt. About ten minutes.

docs.title: 1. Say who the application is
docs.text:
from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec, AppPaths

APP = AppSpec(
    name="Pomodoro",
    app_id="pomodoro",
    version="0.1.0",
    default_config_format="json",
)

app_id is the directory name, so you never type a path. AppSpec is covered in Application identity.

docs.title: 2. Say what it remembers
docs.text:
SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "timer",
            title="Timer",
            options=(
                Option("minutes", int, 25, "Length of a session.", minimum=1, maximum=180),
                Option("label", str, "Focus", "What the session is called."),
                Option("chime", bool, True, "Play a sound at the end."),
                Option("mode", str, "work", "Which mode to start in.",
                       choices=("work", "break")),
            ),
        )
    ]
)

That is the entire specification of what persists: two strings, an integer and a boolean. Each has a default, and three of the four carry a constraint.

docs.title: 3. Open the store
docs.text:
paths = AppPaths.resolve(APP.app_id, config_home=Path("pomodoro-home"))
store = ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, AppContext(APP, paths)).load()

print(store.path)        # pomodoro-home/pomodoro/config.json
print(store.exists())    # False — nothing is written until there is something to write

Two things to notice already:

  • --config-home in the tutorial stands in for $XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Nothing writes to your real ~/.config, which is also what lets the test suite run without side effects.
  • Reading does not create a file. Starting an application should not litter.

docs.title: 4. Read a value: it is already the right type
docs.text:
minutes = store.get("timer.minutes")
print(repr(minutes))     # 25
print(type(minutes).__name__)   # int

There is no getint. There is no int(store.get(...)), no getboolean, and no "true" anywhere in your code. The schema is the only place the type is written down, and the store is where it is applied.

docs.title: 5. Write a value: coercion is the schema's job
docs.text:
store.set("timer.minutes", "50")     # a string, on purpose
store.set("timer.chime", "no")       # also not a boolean
store.save()

Both of those are accepted. Coercion turns "50" into an integer and "no" into False, so a command-line tool, a web form and a config file all work without the caller helping.

$ python examples/tutorials/settings.py
settings live in pomodoro-home/pomodoro/config.json
file exists yet? False
minutes: 25 (int)
after saving: 50, False
problems: none

docs.title: 6. Watch a bad value get refused
docs.text:
Constraints are enforced in two places, and it matters which is which:

When What it does Schema.validate() when you ask reports everything wrong with the data on disk ConfigStore.set() at the call site rejects, and does not store 
$ python examples/tutorials/settings.py --break
refused: timer.minutes: 999 exceeds the maximum of 180
refused: timer.mode: 'siesta' is not one of: work, break
after saving: 50, False

999 is a perfectly good integer. The schema is what refuses it, and the message names the bound rather than saying "invalid". The refused values never reached the file — the saved minutes is still 50.

Why both?

A value can be unacceptable for two different reasons. 999 cannot be coerced — it is a valid integer, just out of range. "lots" cannot be read as an integer at all. Gesso reports them the same way because from the outside they are the same problem: this setting is not usable, and you would rather know now than at three in the morning.

The split matters because validate() has to cope with a file a human edited, while set() is the last moment you have the caller's attention.

docs.title: 7. Change the format without changing the code
docs.text:
reloaded.convert_to("toml")

$ python examples/tutorials/settings.py --toml
rewritten as toml: pomodoro-home/pomodoro/config.toml

The old file is kept as a .bak. And if the format you asked for has no writer installed:

$ python examples/tutorials/settings.py --toml
cannot convert: writing TOML requires the 'tomli-w' package (pip install 'gesso-sdk[toml]')

That is the design, not a shortcoming: a codec that cannot write says so rather than quietly writing a second config file in a format it can manage. Two config files is a bug you find months later.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: store a setting, and refuse a bad one.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/settings.py
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/settings.py --break
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/settings.py --toml
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path

from gesso.config import ConfigError, ConfigStore, Option, Schema, Section
from gesso.core import AppContext, AppSpec, AppPaths

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. What is this, and what does it remember?
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
APP = AppSpec(
    name="Pomodoro",
    app_id="pomodoro",
    version="0.1.0",
    default_config_format="json",
)

SCHEMA = Schema(
    [
        Section(
            "timer",
            title="Timer",
            options=(
                Option("minutes", int, 25, "Length of a session.", minimum=1, maximum=180),
                Option("label", str, "Focus", "What the session is called."),
                Option("chime", bool, True, "Play a sound at the end."),
                Option(
                    "mode",
                    str,
                    "work",
                    "Which mode to start in.",
                    choices=("work", "break"),
                ),
            ),
        )
    ]
)


def open_store(name: str, config_home: Path) -> ConfigStore:
    """Find (or plan) the settings file for an application called *name*."""
    spec = APP if name == APP.app_id else AppSpec(name=name, app_id=name, version="0.1.0")
    paths = AppPaths.resolve(spec.app_id, config_home=config_home)
    return ConfigStore.for_app(SCHEMA, AppContext(spec, paths)).load()


def main(argv: list) -> int:
    config_home = Path("pomodoro-home")
    store = open_store("pomodoro", config_home)
    print(f"settings live in {store.path}")
    print(f"file exists yet? {store.exists()}")

    # Settings come out of the store already typed. There is no getboolean.
    minutes = store.get("timer.minutes")
    print(f"minutes: {minutes!r} ({type(minutes).__name__})")

    if "--break" in argv:
        # A value the schema refuses never reaches the file.
        try:
            store.set("timer.minutes", 999)
        except ConfigError as exc:
            print(f"refused: {exc}")
        try:
            store.set("timer.mode", "siesta")
        except ConfigError as exc:
            print(f"refused: {exc}")

    # A *string* is fine: coercion is the schema's job, not the caller's.
    store.set("timer.minutes", "50")
    store.set("timer.chime", "no")
    store.save()

    reloaded = open_store("pomodoro", config_home)
    print(f"after saving: {reloaded.get('timer.minutes')!r}, {reloaded.get('timer.chime')!r}")

    if "--toml" in argv:
        try:
            reloaded.convert_to("toml")
            print(f"rewritten as {reloaded.format}: {reloaded.path}")
        except ConfigError as exc:
            # A codec that cannot write says which package to install, rather
            # than writing a second config file in a format it can manage.
            print(f"cannot convert: {exc}")

    problems = reloaded.validate()
    print(f"problems: {problems or 'none'}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

docs.title: Translate an application
docs.text:
You will end up with two catalogs, correct plural forms, a language that follows the system when it should, and a user override that wins.

No Qt. About fifteen minutes.

docs.title: 1. Write a catalog
docs.text:
A catalog is JSON, looked up by dotted key. examples/tutorials/locales/en.json:

{
  "greeting": {
    "title": "Pomodoro",
    "hello": "Hello, {name}!",
    "labelled": "Press {key} to continue.",
    "items": {
      "one": "{count} item",
      "other": "{count} items"
    }
  }
}

There is nothing to compile and no .po/.mo step: the catalogs ship as-is and are read at runtime.

docs.title: 2. Point a translator at them
docs.text:
from gesso.i18n import DEFAULT_LANGUAGE, DirectorySource, Translator, detect_language

translator = Translator(
    [DirectorySource(LOCALES, name="application")],
    language=detect_language() or DEFAULT_LANGUAGE,
    fallback=DEFAULT_LANGUAGE,
    include_framework=False,
)

detect_language() reads LANGUAGE, LC_ALL, LC_MESSAGES and LANG, in that order, and returns "" for the values that mean "unset" — C, POSIX, and an unset variable. That is why it is or DEFAULT_LANGUAGE and not a default argument: an empty detection is a real answer, not a missing one.

$ python examples/tutorials/greeting.py
detected from the environment: en
active language:  en

$ LANGUAGE=fr_FR.UTF-8 python examples/tutorials/greeting.py
detected from the environment: fr
active language:  fr

docs.title: 3. Look things up
docs.text:
translator.t("greeting.hello", name="Ada")     # 'Hello, Ada!'

{name} is filled from the keyword arguments. A missing key comes back as itself:

translator.t("greeting.untitled")              # 'greeting.untitled'

Not an empty string — an empty string looks like a layout bug, while a raw key is visible on screen and greppable in your source.

The key argument is positional-only

def t(key_name: str, /, *, default=None, **kwargs) -> str

That / is load-bearing. A translation is allowed to contain a placeholder called key:

"labelled": "Press {key} to continue."

translator.t("greeting.labelled", key="Ctrl+K")   # 'Press Ctrl+K to continue.'

Without the positional-only marker, key="Ctrl+K" would collide with the parameter of the same name and raise got multiple values for argument 'key'. Gesso found this because a real application wanted to say "press {key}".

docs.title: 4. Get plurals right, by hand
docs.text:
Gesso does not guess plural rules. The tutorial makes the consequence explicit:

def count_of(translator, key, count):
    form = "one" if count == 1 else "other"
    return translator.t(f"{key}.{form}", count=count)

  0 -> 0 items
  1 -> 1 item
  2 -> 2 items

This is not laziness, and it is worth understanding before you reach for one/other in a language you do not speak:

Language Plural forms English, French 2 Russian, Polish 3 Arabic 6

Getting those right needs real CLDR data, which Gesso's roadmap lists as a planned optional backend rather than something the core pretends to have. Until then the catalogs carry the forms and your application chooses — which has the side benefit that the rule is visible in your code instead of hidden in a library's tables.

If you only ship English, this is the whole rule and you are done.

docs.title: 5. Let the user override you
docs.text:
Add their directory as a later source:

sources = [DirectorySource(LOCALES, name="application")]
sources.append(DirectorySource(USER_LOCALES, name="user"))

Sources are consulted in ascending priority — later wins:

$ python examples/tutorials/greeting.py --language fr
application only: Pomodoro
with the user's:  Pomodoro (personnalisé)

The fr.json that produced that second line is four lines:

{ "greeting": { "title": "Pomodoro (personnalisé)" } }

In a real application that directory lives beside the user's settings (~/.config/<app>/i18n/), not beside your code. It is next to the tutorial only so the example stands alone. Translator.for_app(context, ...) wires that up for you:

translator = Translator.for_app(context, language=..., locale_dir=LOCALES)

docs.title: 6. And know which way is right-to-left
docs.text:
is_rtl(translator.language)     # False for 'fr', True for 'ar' or 'he'

Gesso ships the language list and the question; it does not flip your window for you. run_app applies the direction to the whole application, because Qt mirrors every widget without any of them knowing — which is the only way it is ever going to be done correctly. See the shell tutorial.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: translate an application, and get plurals right.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/greeting.py
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/greeting.py --language fr
    LANGUAGE=fr_FR.UTF-8 PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/greeting.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from pathlib import Path

from gesso.i18n import (
    DEFAULT_LANGUAGE,
    DirectorySource,
    MappingSource,
    Translator,
    detect_language,
    is_rtl,
    normalize_lang,
)

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
#: The application's catalogs, shipped with the code.
LOCALES = HERE / "locales"
#: A *user's* overrides. Real applications put this beside the user's settings
#: (`~/.config/<app>/i18n/`), not beside their own; it is next to the code here
#: only so the tutorial is self-contained.
USER_LOCALES = HERE / "user-locales"


def build_translator(language: str | None = None, *, user: bool = True) -> Translator:
    """A translator for this tutorial's catalogs.

    Source order is the whole lesson. Sources are consulted in **ascending
    priority**:

    1. Gesso's own `gesso.*` catalogs (skipped here — this app uses none);
    2. the application's, shipped with the code;
    3. the user's, read from beside their settings.

    So a user can override any string without touching the application — the
    same way a user theme overrides a built-in palette.
    """
    sources = [DirectorySource(LOCALES, name="application")]
    if user:
        sources.append(DirectorySource(USER_LOCALES, name="user"))

    return Translator(
        sources,
        language=language or detect_language() or DEFAULT_LANGUAGE,
        fallback=DEFAULT_LANGUAGE,
        include_framework=False,
    )


def count_of(translator: Translator, key: str, count: int) -> str:
    """Choose the ``.one`` or ``.other`` form of *key* for *count*.

    Gesso does not guess plural rules, and this function is the honest
    consequence. English and French really do have two forms; Russian has
    three and Arabic six, and getting those right needs real CLDR data. So the
    catalogs carry the forms and the application picks — which also means the
    rule stays visible in your code instead of hiding in a library's tables.
    """
    form = "one" if count == 1 else "other"
    return translator.t(f"{key}.{form}", count=count)


def main(argv: list) -> int:
    requested = None
    if "--language" in argv:
        requested = argv[argv.index("--language") + 1]

    print(f"detected from the environment: {detect_language() or '(nothing)'}")
    print(f"normalised:                    {normalize_lang('fr_FR.UTF-8')!r}")
    print()

    translator = build_translator(requested)
    print(f"active language:  {translator.language}")
    print(f"right to left?    {is_rtl(translator.language)}")
    print(f"catalogs provide: {translator.languages()}")
    print()

    print(f"  title    {translator.t('greeting.title')}")
    print(f"  hello    {translator.t('greeting.hello', name='Ada')}")
    print(f"  goodbye  {translator.t('greeting.goodbye', name='Ada')}")

    # A placeholder called `key` is safe, because the translation key is
    # positional-only. That is what `t(key_name, /, **kwargs)` is for.
    print(f"  labelled {translator.t('greeting.labelled', key='Ctrl+K')}")

    print("  counts:")
    for count in (0, 1, 2):
        print(f"    {count} -> {count_of(translator, 'greeting.items', count)}")

    # A key nobody defined comes back as *itself*: visible on screen, greppable
    # in the source, and never an empty string that looks like a layout bug.
    print(f"  missing  {translator.t('greeting.untitled')!r}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The user's overrides, which win because they were consulted last
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    application_only = build_translator(requested, user=False)
    print(f"\napplication only: {application_only.t('greeting.title')}")
    print(f"with the user's:  {translator.t('greeting.title')}")

    # A catalog can also live in memory: handy for tests, and for strings that
    # are generated rather than written.
    in_memory = Translator(
        [MappingSource({"en": {"greeting": {"hello": "Hi {name}!"}}})],
        language="en",
        include_framework=False,
    )
    print(f"in memory:        {in_memory.t('greeting.hello', name='Ada')}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

docs.title: The test that actually saves you
docs.text:
A missing translation does not fail. It prints English. Nothing raises, your tests stay green, and the bug ships.

The only cheap defence is comparing the catalogs key-for-key:

def keys_of(catalog, prefix=""):
    found = set()
    for key, value in catalog.items():
        path = f"{prefix}.{key}" if prefix else key
        found |= keys_of(value, path) if isinstance(value, dict) else {path}
    return found


def test_the_catalogs_cover_the_same_keys():
    assert keys_of(load_catalog("en")) == keys_of(load_catalog("fr"))

Two more from the examples are worth stealing:

# Every key resolves, rather than coming back as itself.
unresolved = [k for k in sorted(keys_of(catalog)) if translator.t(k) == k]
assert unresolved == []

That one catches a dotted key name written inside JSON. "theme.help": "…" is a literal key, not a nested one, so the lookup walks into the string "Palette" and gives up — silently. Tracker shipped five of those until a test like this found them.

docs.title: Ship your own icons
docs.text:
You will end up with your own artwork, tinted by whichever theme is active, in the same set as Gesso's.

Qt required. About ten minutes.

docs.title: 1. Draw one, and put it in a directory
docs.text:
Any SVG will do. examples/tutorials/icons/star.svg:

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24" viewBox="0 0 24 24"
     fill="none" stroke="#9a9a9a" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round">
  <path d="M12 3l2.6 5.6 6 .8-4.4 4.2 1.1 6-5.3-3-5.3 3 1.1-6L3.4 9.4l6-.8z" />
</svg>

The stroke colour does not matter

Gesso tints by composition, not by editing SVG source: it draws the artwork, then CompositionMode_SourceIn replaces the colour while keeping the alpha. So stroke="#9a9a9a" above is never seen, and one asset serves every theme.

That is the whole reason a theme switch does not need a second copy of your icons — which is exactly what a set of fixed-colour icons makes you do.

docs.title: 2. Register the directory
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.icons import IconRegistry

mine = IconRegistry([MY_ICONS])
print(mine.names())        # ['star']
print(mine.has("check"))   # False

Careful. That registry knows about your icons and nothing else:

my directory alone provides: ['star']
  knows 'check'?  False

This is the mistake to know about before you make it. The base stylesheet addresses some icons by name — the spin-box arrows are chevron-up and chevron-down — so a registry that replaced Gesso's would leave them unresolved in your application, at runtime, silently.

Layer instead:

layered = IconRegistry([GESSO_ICONS])
layered.add_directory(MY_ICONS)      # appended, so later wins

layered: 13 icons
  knows 'check'?  True   (Gesso's, still there)
  knows 'star'?   True    (mine, added)

Directories are searched in reverse order, so yours wins for any name the two share. That is how you override Gesso's artwork without forking it.

docs.title: 3. Make typos loud
docs.text:
layered.source("str")

no icon named 'str'; available icons: check, chevron-down, chevron-left,
chevron-right, chevron-up, close, info, minus, plus, refresh, search, star, warning

A missing icon names the alternatives rather than returning a blank pixmap or raising a bare KeyError. "no icon called 'str'" is a typo you want to see immediately, and a list of what does exist usually contains the answer.

docs.title: 4. Ask for a role, not a colour
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.icons import ROLE_TOKENS
Role Token For idle text_muted a resting icon strong text one that should stand out active accent selected disabled text_disabled unavailable on-accent accent_text sitting on an accent-coloured surface

Because each role names a token rather than a colour, one asset is correct in every theme:

dark   idle=#9a9a9a  active=#7c6cf6
light  idle=#6a6a72  active=#5b4bd6

Those values come out of whichever palette is applied. Add a theme and your icons follow it; you do not touch the icons.

docs.title: 5. Attach them to a theme
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.icons import ThemedIcons
from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager

themes = ThemeManager(app)
icons = ThemedIcons(layered, themes)

icons.render_pixmap("star", role="active", size=24)
icons.make_icon("star", role="idle", size=18)     # a QIcon

docs.title: 6. And repaint them when the theme moves
docs.text:
This is the part people miss.

An icon is rendered into a QPixmap. A QLabel holds that pixmap. A pixmap does not know the theme moved, so changing palette leaves every icon at its old colour unless something rebuilds it:

icons.iconsChanged.connect(repaint_everything)

ThemedIcons emits iconsChanged after a theme change. It says when; your application decides what. Anything holding an icon has to do something:

  • a widget built from a name — IconButton.set_role(role) re-renders it;
  • a label holding a pixmap — call render_pixmap again.

Gallery demonstrates both, in one window you can switch palettes under.

The alternative, and why it is worse

Gesso could have had icons register themselves and repaint automatically. It does not, because that would mean every icon widget holds a reference to the theme manager, and your widgets would have to be Gesso's widgets. The signal keeps the dependency one-way: Gesso says when, you say what.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: ship your own icons, tinted by the theme.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/icons.py
    QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/icons.py

(``offscreen`` is only needed on a machine with no display; the script prints a
report and never opens a window.)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

from gesso.ui.icons import ROLE_TOKENS, IconError, IconRegistry, ThemedIcons
from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager

HERE = Path(__file__).parent
#: This application's own icons.
MY_ICONS = HERE / "icons"
#: Gesso's, which this application wants to keep.
import gesso.ui.icons  # noqa: E402  (after the constants, for readability)

GESSO_ICONS = gesso.ui.icons.ICONS_DIR


def main() -> int:
    from gesso.ui.app import create_app

    app = create_app(_spec(), [])

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. A registry is a search path, and later directories win
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    mine_only = IconRegistry([MY_ICONS])
    print(f"my directory alone provides: {mine_only.names()}")

    # ...which means Gesso's icons are now *gone*. This is the mistake to know
    # about: the stylesheet addresses some icons by name (the spin-box arrows),
    # so a registry that replaced Gesso's would leave them unresolved.
    print(f"  knows 'check'?  {mine_only.has('check')}")
    print(f"  knows 'star'?   {mine_only.has('star')}")

    layered = IconRegistry([GESSO_ICONS])
    layered.add_directory(MY_ICONS)
    print(f"\nlayered: {len(layered.names())} icons")
    print(f"  knows 'check'?  {layered.has('check')}   (Gesso's, still there)")
    print(f"  knows 'star'?   {layered.has('star')}    (mine, added)")

    # A name that does not exist says so, and lists what does — because
    # "no icon called 'str'" is a typo you want to see immediately.
    try:
        layered.source("str")
    except IconError as exc:
        print(f"\ntypos are loud: {exc}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Roles are tokens, not colours
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\nroles map to tokens, so one piece of artwork suits every theme:")
    for role, token in sorted(ROLE_TOKENS.items()):
        print(f"  {role:<10} -> {token}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. ThemedIcons resolves those at render time
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    themes = ThemeManager(app, parent=app)
    icons = ThemedIcons(layered, themes)

    for name in ("dark", "light"):
        themes.apply(name)
        tinted = {role: icons.color(role) for role in icons.roles()}
        print(f"\n{name:<6} idle={tinted['idle']}  active={tinted['active']}")

    pixmap = icons.render_pixmap("star", role="active", size=24)
    print(f"\nrendered 'star' at 24px: {pixmap.width()}x{pixmap.height()}, null? {pixmap.isNull()}")

    # `iconsChanged` fires after every theme change. It says *when* the icons
    # are stale; whatever is displaying them decides what to rebuild — a QLabel
    # holds a pixmap, and a pixmap does not know the theme moved.
    fired = []
    icons.iconsChanged.connect(lambda: fired.append(True))
    themes.apply("dark")
    themes.apply("light")
    print(f"iconsChanged fired {len(fired)} times across two theme changes")
    return 0


def _spec():
    from gesso.core import AppSpec

    return AppSpec(name="Icons", app_id="icons-tutorial", version="0.1.0")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.title: Build a windowed application
docs.text:
You will end up with two pages, a header button, a live status line and a theme — without writing the sidebar, the navigation, the page stack or a single line of styling.

Qt required. About fifteen minutes. This is the tutorial the Tracker example is built on.

docs.title: 1. The entry point is one call
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.app import run_app

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(run_app(APP, build))

run_app does everything a Qt application does slightly differently in every project:

What it does create_app makes the QApplication and sets its metadata from the AppSpec layout direction mirrors the whole interface if the language is right-to-left theme makes a ThemeManager, applies the stored or given palette palette sets the QPalette, so native furniture matches icons makes a ThemedIcons over Gesso's icons plus any icon_dirs exception hook shows an error raised inside a slot, instead of swallowing it window makes the shell, calls build, shows it, runs the loop

That exception hook is the one people never write and always need. Without it, an exception in a Qt slot is printed to a terminal nobody is reading, and the application carries on looking fine.

docs.title: 2. A page is an ordinary widget
docs.text:
class HomePage(QWidget):
    def __init__(self, icons, *, on_change=None, parent=None):
        super().__init__(parent)
        ...

No base class. No registration. No decorator. A page is a QWidget, and the shell wraps it in a header and gives it a navigation entry.

The two methods below are conventions, not Gesso types — but they are worth adopting, because they are the only two questions the shell needs answered:

def header_actions(self):
    """Buttons this page wants in its header."""
    button = IconButton("plus", icons=self.icons, tooltip="Add a note")
    button.clicked.connect(self.add_note)
    return [button]

The page says which buttons it wants. The shell decides where they go. The page never learns where that was — which is why it keeps working when the layout changes.

def retranslate(self):
    """Say everything again, in whatever language is now active."""

Optional, and only needed if your strings come from a catalog. See step 6.

docs.title: 3. Tell the shell what to show
docs.text:
def build(shell):
    home = HomePage(shell.icons, on_change=lambda: shell.set_info(f"{home.count()} notes"))

    shell.set_brand(APP.display_name, "two pages, one call to run_app")

    shell.add_page(
        "home", "Home", home,
        comment="Your notes live here.",
        icon="check",
        actions=home.header_actions(),
    )
    shell.add_page("about", "About", AboutPage(), comment="What this is.", icon="info")

    shell.set_message("Ready.")
    shell.set_info("0 notes")

add_page does more than it looks like:

  • wraps your widget in a header carrying the title and comment;
  • creates the navigation entry, with the icon, in the same call;
  • adds the page to the content stack;
  • keeps the navigation button's checked state in step with the visible page.

That last point is why the navigation is not hard-coded anywhere: a page and its destination are created together, so the two cannot drift apart.

shell.icons and shell.theme_manager are ready by the time build is called, so a page can be handed them without the application building its own.

docs.title: 4. The status bar has two halves
docs.text:
shell.set_message("Ready.")       # left: transient, e.g. "Saved."
shell.set_info("0 notes")         # right: standing information

set_message takes an optional timeout in milliseconds and reverts afterwards, which is what you want for "Downloaded 12 images." set_info is for the state of the world, and it stays put.

docs.title: 5. Do not reach for the shell from inside a page
docs.text:
Notice the shape in step 3:

on_change=lambda: shell.set_info(f"{home.count()} notes")

The page reports that something happened; the application decides what that means. The alternative — the page walking up to its window with self.window().set_info(...) — couples every page to the shell, and is exactly what makes a UI hard to test in isolation. HomePage in the tutorial has no idea it is inside a shell.

docs.title: 6. And a language you can change live
docs.text:
If your strings come from a catalog, changing language needs three things, and the shell provides two of them:

def retranslate():
    shell.set_brand(APP.display_name, session.t("app.tagline"))
    # A page's title lives in the Page record, the navigation button AND the
    # header. Retitling two of three is worse than retitling none.
    shell.set_page_title("home", session.t("app.nav.home"), session.t("app.page.home"))
    # Gesso's own strings, under the reserved `gesso.` domain.
    shell.retranslate()
    for page in pages.values():
        page.retranslate()

And when you build the application, hand the shell your translator:

run_app(APP, build, translate=t)

That is what makes shell.retranslate() come out in the right language rather than English. Gesso's own strings live under gesso.* — a reserved domain the framework owns and your catalogs cannot collide with — and a missing translation shows the raw key rather than an empty label, so you can see it on screen and grep for it.

docs.title: 7. A window of your own, if you need one
docs.text:
build may return a window instead of populating the shell:

def build(shell):
    return MyOwnWindow()

run_app shows that instead. (Return a QWidget or nothing — anything else is a mistake, and run_app says so rather than failing inside Qt's start-up.) Returning one is rarely right, but it is the escape hatch when the shell's shape genuinely does not fit.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: a windowed application, in one call.

This is the whole shell. Two pages, a header button, a status line, and a theme
— and none of the sidebar, navigation, page-stack or styling code that would
usually go with them.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/window.py
    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/window.py --theme light
    QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/window.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
from typing import Any, List, Optional, Sequence

from PySide6.QtWidgets import QLabel, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from gesso.core import AppSpec
from gesso.ui.app import run_app
from gesso.ui.widgets import Card, EmptyState, IconButton, SettingRow, ToggleButton

APP = AppSpec(
    name="Notes",
    app_id="notes-tutorial",
    org="Tutorial",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="Two pages and a window, in one call.",
)

#: ``--check`` builds everything and closes immediately instead of entering the
#: event loop. Useful in CI, and it is how the tutorial is tested.
CHECK = "--check" in sys.argv[1:]


class HomePage(QWidget):
    """A page is an ordinary widget.

    It does not know it is a page: no base class, no registration. The shell
    wraps it in a header and gives it a navigation entry.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        icons: Any,
        *,
        on_change: Optional[Any] = None,
        parent: Optional[QWidget] = None,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(parent)
        self.notes: List[str] = []
        # Kept because an IconButton given a *name* needs the icon set to
        # resolve it — `icons=...` — and the error message says exactly that.
        self.icons = icons
        # The page reports that something happened; the application decides what
        # that means. It never reaches for the shell itself.
        self.on_change = on_change

        layout = QVBoxLayout(self)
        layout.setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
        layout.setSpacing(12)

        self.card = Card(margins=20, spacing=8)
        layout.addWidget(self.card)
        layout.addStretch(1)
        self.render()

    def header_actions(self) -> List[QWidget]:
        """Buttons this page wants in its header.

        Not a Gesso type and not a shell feature — just the convention this
        application uses. The shell is told `actions=page.header_actions()` and
        the page never learns where they ended up.
        """
        button = IconButton("plus", icons=self.icons, tooltip="Add a note")
        button.clicked.connect(self.add_note)
        return [button]

    def add_note(self) -> None:
        self.notes.append(f"Note {len(self.notes) + 1}")
        self.render()
        if self.on_change is not None:
            self.on_change()

    def count(self) -> int:
        return len(self.notes)

    def render(self) -> None:
        while self.card.body.count():
            item = self.card.body.takeAt(0)
            widget = item.widget()
            if widget is not None:
                widget.hide()
                widget.setParent(None)
                widget.deleteLater()

        if not self.notes:
            self.card.body.addWidget(
                EmptyState("No notes yet. Use the + button in the header.")
            )
            return
        for note in self.notes:
            self.card.body.addWidget(SettingRow(note, QLabel("saved")))


class AboutPage(QWidget):
    """A second page, to prove the navigation is not hard-coded."""

    def __init__(self, parent: Optional[QWidget] = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(parent)
        layout = QVBoxLayout(self)
        layout.setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)

        card = Card(margins=24, spacing=8)

        title = QLabel(APP.display_name)
        title.setObjectName("displayTitle")
        card.body.addWidget(title)

        blurb = QLabel(APP.description)
        blurb.setObjectName("pageSubtitle")
        blurb.setWordWrap(True)
        card.body.addWidget(blurb)

        self.notify = ToggleButton("Notify me", checked=False)
        card.body.addWidget(SettingRow("Notifications", self.notify))

        layout.addWidget(card)
        layout.addStretch(1)


def build(shell: Any) -> None:
    """Populate the shell. Called once, after the window exists.

    ``shell`` is an ``AppShell``: it already has a sidebar, a drawer button, a
    content stack, a status bar and a theme applied. This function only says
    what goes in them.
    """

    def refresh_status() -> None:
        shell.set_info(f"{home.count()} notes")

    home = HomePage(shell.icons, on_change=refresh_status)

    shell.set_brand(APP.display_name, "two pages, one call to run_app")

    shell.add_page(
        "home",
        "Home",
        home,
        comment="Your notes live here.",
        icon="check",
        actions=home.header_actions(),
    )
    shell.add_page(
        "about",
        "About",
        AboutPage(),
        comment="What this is.",
        icon="info",
    )

    # The status bar: a short-lived message on the left, standing information on
    # the right.
    shell.set_message("Ready.")
    refresh_status()

    if CHECK:
        from PySide6.QtCore import QTimer

        QTimer.singleShot(0, shell.close)


def main(argv: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> int:
    return run_app(
        APP,
        build,
        argv=argv,
        theme=None,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.title: Make a palette
docs.text:
You will end up with a palette that states only what it wants to change, and a rendered stylesheet — checked without opening a window.

No Qt at all. About ten minutes.

This runs without a toolkit

The token contract and the stylesheet renderer are Qt-free. That is deliberate, and this tutorial proves it: at the end the script prints which PySide6 modules it loaded, and the answer is none.

You can therefore check a palette on a build server, in a pre-commit hook, or while your GUI dependencies are still installing.

docs.title: 1. See what you can set
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.theme import BASE_CONTRACT, TOKEN_GROUPS

print(len(BASE_CONTRACT), "tokens in", len(TOKEN_GROUPS), "groups")
for group, tokens in BASE_CONTRACT.groups().items():
    print(f"  {group:<9} {', '.join(t.key for t in tokens)}")

the contract declares 30 tokens in 9 groups:
  surfaces  window, panel, card, card_hover, preview_bg, menu_bg, nav_active_bg, tooltip_bg
  text      text_strong, text, text_muted, text_disabled, tooltip_text
  accent    accent, accent_hover, accent_text, selection
  buttons   btn_bg, btn_hover, btn_active
  borders   border, border_strong
  inputs    input_bg, input_border, focus_border
  scroll    scroll_handle, scroll_handle_hover
  menu      menu_hover
  status    status_bg, status_text

Thirty is a deliberately small number. A token earns its place by appearing in the stylesheet, and the stylesheet only covers the widgets Gesso actually ships — so there are no tokens for things that do not exist yet.

docs.title: 2. A palette is a JSON file, and it may be short
docs.text:
{
  "name": "Midnight",
  "description": "Tracker's own palette.",
  "colors": {
    "window": "#15161e",
    "panel": "#1b1d27",
    "card": "#22242f",
    "text_strong": "#eef1ff",
    "accent": "#7aa2f7",
    "accent_text": "#101223"
  }
}

Six of thirty. The other twenty-four are not missing — the contract has a last-resort default for every token:

resolved = BASE_CONTRACT.resolve(PARTIAL)
print(len(resolved))                       # 30
print(resolved["window"])                  # #15161e  (given)
print(resolved["scroll_handle"])           # #4a4a4a  (from the contract)

That is what makes a palette this short possible. You state what you want to change; everything else keeps working.

docs.title: 3. Know the difference between a typo and a gap
docs.text:
They are different problems with different fixes, so they are reported separately:

unknown tokens: ['acccent']
missing tokens: 24
  • unknown — a key the contract does not define. A misspelt token would otherwise be silently dropped, and you would spend an afternoon wondering why one colour never changes. This is always a bug.
  • missing — a token the palette does not state. Usually fine; sometimes you meant to set it. Use problems(name) when you want to know whether a palette is complete, and --verbose style reporting when you want to know what it leaves to the contract.

docs.title: 4. Render the stylesheet
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.theme import QssError, render

colors = BASE_CONTRACT.resolve(PARTIAL)
try:
    render(colors)
except QssError as exc:
    print(f"render refused: {exc}")

render refused: the stylesheet needs tokens that were not provided: icon_dir

Exactly one placeholder in the stylesheet is not a token: icon_dir, a filesystem path, because QSS wants a path and not a colour. Pass it alongside:

sheet = render(colors, {"icon_dir": "/usr/share/gesso/icons"})
print(len(sheet))          # 9460
print("#7aa2f7" in sheet)  # True

Render fails loudly, and that is the point

string.Template.substitute raises on the first gap it meets. That is a feature: a stylesheet that silently lost its focus ring, or a palette that quietly failed to apply, is the kind of bug that is found by a user rather than by you.

It is also why the checks in steps 2 and 3 exist — so you meet the problem here, in a script, rather than there, in a window.

docs.title: 5. Hand the palette to a manager
docs.text:
ThemeManager is the Qt half. It renders the stylesheet and builds a QPalette, so natively-drawn furniture — tooltips, text selection, menu shadows — matches the theme instead of falling back to the platform default:

from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager

manager = ThemeManager(app, user_dir=paths.config_dir / "themes", seed=True)
manager.apply("midnight")

seed=True copies each built-in palette into the user's directory once, so the theme is discoverable and therefore editable. Copies are only written where nothing exists, so a later release cannot silently undo someone's customisation.

Search order, in ascending priority: the built-ins, then the user's directory. Exactly the same shape as translation catalogs.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: the token contract, without a toolkit.

This is the whole theming layer minus Qt. Nothing here imports PySide6, so you
can check a palette on a build server, in a pre-commit hook, or while your GUI
dependencies are still installing.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/palette.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from gesso.ui.theme import BASE_CONTRACT, QssError, TOKEN_GROUPS, render

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. A palette only has to state what it changes
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tracker's actual palette, trimmed to the interesting lines. The other
# fourteen tokens are not missing: the contract has a last-resort default for
# every one of them, which is what lets a palette be this short.
PARTIAL = {
    "window": "#15161e",
    "panel": "#1b1d27",
    "card": "#22242f",
    "text_strong": "#eef1ff",
    "accent": "#7aa2f7",
    "accent_text": "#101223",
}


def main() -> int:
    print(f"the contract declares {len(BASE_CONTRACT)} tokens in {len(TOKEN_GROUPS)} groups:")
    for group, tokens in BASE_CONTRACT.groups().items():
        print(f"  {group:<9} {', '.join(token.key for token in tokens)}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Resolving fills the gaps
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    resolved = BASE_CONTRACT.resolve(PARTIAL)
    print(f"\n{PARTIAL.__len__()} given + contract defaults = {len(resolved)} tokens")
    print(f"  window        {resolved['window']}   (given)")
    print(f"  scroll_handle {resolved['scroll_handle']}   (from the contract)")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Typos and gaps are reported, not ignored
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # A mistyped token is *unknown*: it would be silently dropped otherwise, and
    # you would spend an afternoon wondering why one colour never changes.
    print(f"\nunknown tokens: {BASE_CONTRACT.unknown({'acccent': '#fff'})}")
    # An unstated one is *missing*, which is a different problem with a
    # different fix.
    print(f"missing tokens: {len(BASE_CONTRACT.missing(PARTIAL))}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Rendering the stylesheet
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    colors = BASE_CONTRACT.resolve(PARTIAL)
    try:
        render(colors)
    except QssError as exc:
        # Exactly one placeholder is not a token: `icon_dir`, a filesystem path
        # the stylesheet uses for the spin-box arrows.
        print(f"\nrender refused: {exc}")

    sheet = render(colors, {"icon_dir": "/usr/share/gesso/icons"})
    print(f"rendered {len(sheet)} characters of QSS")
    print(f"  accent made it into the sheet: {'#7aa2f7' in sheet}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. And no Qt anywhere
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    import sys

    loaded = [name for name in sys.modules if name.startswith("PySide6")]
    print(f"\nPySide6 modules loaded: {loaded or 'none'}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

docs.title: Build a settings pane
docs.text:
You will end up with a pane built from Gesso's widgets and styled by the base stylesheet — with no stylesheet of your own.

Qt required. About fifteen minutes.

docs.title: 1. The one rule
docs.text:
Every widget in the library sets its own object name, and the stylesheet matches on that name. The application writes no QSS. That is the whole idea; the rest of this tutorial is what it buys you.

The names are also deliberately unqualified. The stylesheet says #card, not QFrame#card, so a QLabel can be a card if you want one to be.

docs.title: 2. Put widgets in a card
docs.text:
from gesso.ui.widgets import Card, PageHeader, SegmentedControl, SettingRow, ToggleButton

header = PageHeader("Preferences", "Built from Gesso's widgets.")
self.refresh = IconButton("refresh", icons=icons, tooltip="Reset to defaults")
header.add_action(self.refresh)

general = Card(margins=20, spacing=6)
general.body.addWidget(heading("General"))

PageHeader takes a title, a comment and a list of actions — and add_action puts a widget at the right-hand end of the row. The caller never positions anything, which is why it works on a narrow window.

Card gives you a styled surface and a body layout. That is all it is.

docs.title: 3. Rows are the unit of a settings pane
docs.text:
self.theme = SegmentedControl(["Dark", "Light"])
self.theme.set_value("Dark")
general.body.addWidget(
    SettingRow("Theme", self.theme, "A SegmentedControl as the row's control.")
)

self.notify = ToggleButton("On", checked=True)
general.body.addWidget(
    SettingRow("Notifications", self.notify, "A ToggleButton, and a description.")
)

general.body.addWidget(
    SettingRow("Download folder", QLabel("~/Pictures"), "A plain QLabel is fine.")
)

The third one is the important one. Any QWidget can be the right-hand side of a row — there is no SettingRow.with_text(), no SettingRow.with_segmented_control(). A label, a combo box, a spin box, or a widget you wrote yourself all work, because a row is a label, an optional description, and a control.

SegmentedControl takes either "value" or ("value", "Label") per option, and emits changed with the value:

self.theme.changed.connect(self.on_theme)

It also has set_value, values(), value(), and set_enabled_values([...]) — for greying out the choices that do not apply right now without rebuilding the control.

docs.title: 4. Empty is not an error
docs.text:
advanced.body.addWidget(
    EmptyState("Nothing advanced yet — this is what goes here when there is.")
)

EmptyState is a distinct widget because "there is nothing here yet" is a different message from "something went wrong", and it should not be dressed as one. It is muted and centred; an error should be neither.

docs.title: 5. Check you did not invent a name
docs.text:
The widget library and the stylesheet agree on the object names, and you can check that agreement from your own code:

names = sorted(
    {child.objectName() for child in pane.findChildren(QWidget) if child.objectName()}
)
sheet = themes.stylesheet()
unstyled = [name for name in names if f"#{name}" not in sheet]
print(f"unstyled: {unstyled or 'none — every name has a rule'}")

object names declared by this pane:
  #card
  #emptyState
  #iconButton
  #pageComment
  #pageHeader
  #rowDesc
  #rowLabel
  #sectionTitle
  #segGroup
  #toggleButton

unstyled: none - every name has a rule

Run it after every change. If you add a widget and a name appears in the first list but not in the stylesheet, you have found a hole — either in your code or in Gesso's — before a user finds it as "one panel looks wrong".

What the check is really for

Adding a widget that is unstyled does not raise, log or warn. It simply looks slightly wrong, in one theme, on one screen. This is the cheapest possible way to notice.

docs.title: 6. Show it
docs.text:
app = create_app(APP, [])
themes = ThemeManager(app, parent=app)
themes.apply("dark")                      # light or dark, both are fine
icons = ThemedIcons(theme_manager=themes)

window = QMainWindow()
window.setCentralWidget(SettingsPane(icons))
window.show()
return app.exec()

Note the order: apply the theme before you build the widgets. Widgets created first would paint with the default palette and then be repainted, which is a visible flash on a slow machine.

docs.title: The whole tutorial
docs.text:
"""Tutorial: build a settings pane from the widget library.

Every widget used here sets its **own object name**, and the base stylesheet
matches on that name. This file contains no QSS at all — which is the point.

Run it::

    PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/pane.py
    QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen PYTHONPATH=src python examples/tutorials/pane.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys

from PySide6.QtWidgets import QLabel, QMainWindow, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from gesso.core import AppSpec
from gesso.ui.app import create_app
from gesso.ui.icons import ThemedIcons
from gesso.ui.theme import ThemeManager
from gesso.ui.widgets import (
    Card,
    EmptyState,
    IconButton,
    PageHeader,
    SegmentedControl,
    SettingRow,
    ToggleButton,
)

APP = AppSpec(
    name="Pane",
    app_id="pane-tutorial",
    org="Tutorial",
    version="0.1.0",
    description="A settings pane built from the widget library.",
)

#: ``--check`` builds everything and closes immediately instead of entering the
#: event loop. Useful in CI, and it is how the tutorial is tested.
CHECK = "--check" in sys.argv[1:]


def heading(text: str) -> QLabel:
    """A heading inside a card. ``sectionTitle`` is a *shared* name.

    Gesso's own application shell uses it for page headers, which is why this
    label needs no styling of its own: the rule already exists.
    """
    label = QLabel(text)
    label.setObjectName("sectionTitle")
    return label


class SettingsPane(QWidget):
    """A settings pane, from primitives."""

    def __init__(self, icons: ThemedIcons, parent: QWidget | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(parent)

        layout = QVBoxLayout(self)
        layout.setContentsMargins(24, 20, 24, 20)
        layout.setSpacing(16)

        # A header, with a button the pane itself never positions.
        header = PageHeader(
            "Preferences",
            "Built from Gesso's widgets, with no stylesheet of its own.",
        )
        self.refresh = IconButton("refresh", icons=icons, tooltip="Reset to defaults")
        header.add_action(self.refresh)
        layout.addWidget(header)

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # A card of rows
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        general = Card(margins=20, spacing=6)
        general.body.addWidget(heading("General"))

        self.theme = SegmentedControl(["Dark", "Light"])
        self.theme.set_value("Dark")
        general.body.addWidget(
            SettingRow("Theme", self.theme, "A SegmentedControl as the row's control.")
        )

        self.notify = ToggleButton("On", checked=True)
        general.body.addWidget(
            SettingRow("Notifications", self.notify, "A ToggleButton, and a description.")
        )

        # Any widget can be the control. There is no `SettingRow.with_text()`.
        general.body.addWidget(
            SettingRow("Download folder", QLabel("~/Pictures"), "A plain QLabel is fine.")
        )
        layout.addWidget(general)

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # And an empty state, which is not an error state
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        advanced = Card(margins=20, spacing=6)
        advanced.body.addWidget(heading("Advanced"))
        advanced.body.addWidget(
            EmptyState("Nothing advanced yet — this is what goes here when there is.")
        )
        layout.addWidget(advanced)

        layout.addStretch(1)


def main() -> int:
    app = create_app(APP, [])

    themes = ThemeManager(app, parent=app)
    themes.apply("dark")
    icons = ThemedIcons(theme_manager=themes)

    pane = SettingsPane(icons)
    window = QMainWindow()
    window.setWindowTitle(APP.display_name)
    window.setCentralWidget(pane)
    window.resize(760, 620)
    window.show()

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # What the pane actually declared
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # These names are the public contract between the widget library and the
    # stylesheet. Printing them is the quickest way to notice that a widget you
    # added is unstyled: it will not appear here.
    names = sorted(
        {child.objectName() for child in pane.findChildren(QWidget) if child.objectName()}
    )
    print("object names declared by this pane:")
    for name in names:
        print(f"  #{name}")

    sheet = themes.stylesheet()
    unstyled = [name for name in names if f"#{name}" not in sheet]
    print(f"\nunstyled: {unstyled or 'none - every name has a rule'}")

    if CHECK:
        from PySide6.QtCore import QTimer

        QTimer.singleShot(0, window.close)
    return app.exec()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
